Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply) moved that the house go into committee at the next sitting to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a measure to amend the National Housing Act, 1944, and more particularly; to increase the ratio of loan to lending value under part I of the act, to include under part I houses having two family housing units, of which one is to be occupied *by the owner, to extend the period of amortization of home ownership and rental housing project loans to thirty years, to empower life insurance, trust and loan companies to purchase, improve and sell land to be used for residential housing developments, and to authorize Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to guarantee to such companies the return of the principal invested in such land and improvements, together with interest thereon at a rate not to exceed two per centum per annum.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Canada's part in settlements
On the orders of the day:

subtopic: MEETING OF FOREIGN MINISTERS AT MOSCOW-
speechtext:
I should like to ask a question of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In view of the fact
[The Deputy Chairman.]
that the council of foreign ministers at Moscow are about to abandon their present proceedings, perhaps,, as reports indicate, to meet again in London in the summer, can the minister indicate whether there is any change in the Russian opposition to Canada's fuller participation in the peace settlements, and what are the prospects of Canada's playing a larger part at future meetings of the kind?
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs): There has been nothing determined yet by the council of foreign ministers as to what will be the participation of the other allies in the preparation of the peace settlements for Germany and Austria. There has been some indication of willingness to have the belligerent allies, and even those who merely declared war against Germany, associated in some manner with the preparation of these settlements. The extent to which the Russian foreign minister or his deputy has been willing to go in the meetings has not yet been regarded as satisfactory by the others attending the meetings and for that reason no agreement has been reached. There is the prospect of Canada and the other belligerent allies, even the others who took no active part in the fighting but who declared war against the axis powers, being associated in some degree in the work to be done. But that degree has not been regarded by the other three foreign ministers as sufficient to justify them in accepting it.

subtopic: MOVEMENT OF UNEMPLOYED PERSONS TO EMPLOYMENT IN OTHER AREAS

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: MOVEMENT OF UNEMPLOYED PERSONS TO EMPLOYMENT IN OTHER AREAS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to ask a question of the Minister of Labour? It arises out of a telegram I received from the president of the United Mine Workers of America in Nova Scotia. Has the minister been advised that 1,600 coal miners and their families are prepared to go to central Canada to take other employment if suitable arrangements can be made? If the minister has received that information, does his department contemplate taking any action with respect to it?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: MOVEMENT OF UNEMPLOYED PERSONS TO EMPLOYMENT IN OTHER AREAS
speechtext:
I have not only received the wire but I have replied to it. The wire I received read as follows:
Phalen Local in regular session today prepared to transfer 1,600 men and their families to central in accordance with proposition-
What proposition I do not know.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: MOVEMENT OF UNEMPLOYED PERSONS TO EMPLOYMENT IN OTHER AREAS
speechtext: The one you made in the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: MOVEMENT OF UNEMPLOYED PERSONS TO EMPLOYMENT IN OTHER AREAS
speechtext:
The telegram continues:
Advise if transportation will be paid for families.	.
This is the text of my reply:
In Cape Breton the programme upon which the employment service has been engaged has been to register unemployed persons for whom employment is not available in the province and who are willing and capable of taking steady employment offered in central Canada. In such instances when employment is secured and accepted the transportation of the worker to the job is being paid by the employment service. In consequence of housing difficulties employment opportunities available at the present time are for single men or in the cases with dependents, for men willing to take jobs and await removal of families until they can secure accommodation at their new location.
I should point out that it is not the policy to pay travelling expenses of families. That should be clearly understood. My reply continues:
Transportation costs will not be paid for persons who are temporarily unemployed by
reason of a current strike or other work stoppage of a similar nature as there is work available for them in the local area. I want to make this clear because, as I understand, the number of 1,600 men mentioned in your wire includes men whose employment is affected by the current mining strike. The local employment officers at Glace Bay and Sydney will register unemployed persons wishing to secure employment outside the maritimes and who are eligible for transportation to the places of employment.
I would advise that each application from an unemployed person in the area for employment outside the area will be dealt with by the employment officers in the light of the policy which was outlined in the house by me on Wednesday.

subtopic: MOVEMENT OF UNEMPLOYED PERSONS TO EMPLOYMENT IN OTHER AREAS
speechtext: Has the minister given consideration to the advisability of providing employment within the province rather than facilitating this drain on the population in that part of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: MOVEMENT OF UNEMPLOYED PERSONS TO EMPLOYMENT IN OTHER AREAS
speechtext: I would say to my hon. friend that in the last five years I have moved tens of thousands of people from different parts of Canada. I think it can be truthfully said that many members of this house have also moved to other locations during the war in search of employment-or seats, as my colleague suggests-because it was to their advantage. The same thing happened in Great Britain, the United States and other countries which had built up an enormous war machine during the war years. Just as we provided for the movement of population during those years it will be necessary to provide for the movement of population under present conditions. I think that is elementary; it is simple common sense. But my hon. friend can rest assured1 that the employment service in the maritimes will use every effort to secure employment in that area for those who are unemployed.

subtopic: MOVEMENT OF UNEMPLOYED PERSONS TO EMPLOYMENT IN OTHER AREAS
speechtext: Will transportation be provided by the government to the place of employment for persons in New Brunswick who are unemployed and who are prepared to accept employment that is offered elsewhere? The minister has referred to people employed in Nova Scotia, but does the statement he made on April 16 apply only to that province? Does it include unemployed in New Brunswick?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: MOVEMENT OF UNEMPLOYED PERSONS TO EMPLOYMENT IN OTHER AREAS
speechtext:
As my hon. friend is well aware, my department is not in the business of providing Cook's tours for everybody in Canada. There must be a measure of control over the situation. The policy up to the present has been to restrict the provision of transportation to areas in which the employment conditions are acute, such for instance
Inquiries of the Ministry

as Vancouver a little over a year ago, and recently in the city of Windsor; also in Cape Breton. I think my hon. friend will agree that there must be some control and common sense exercised in the application of the policy.

subtopic: MOVEMENT OF UNEMPLOYED PERSONS TO EMPLOYMENT IN OTHER AREAS
speechtext: I should like to ask a supplementary question of the Minister of Labour arising, out of the answer he gave a moment ago. Does this effort to move large numbers of Nova Scotia miners mean that the government has abandoned its effort of trying to deal on the spot with this Nova Scotia coal problem? If it does not mean that, just what does it mean? The implications to me are very far reaching.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: MOVEMENT OF UNEMPLOYED PERSONS TO EMPLOYMENT IN OTHER AREAS
speechtext: If my hon. friend had listened to what I said he would have, had a clear understanding of what I implied, and if he will take the trouble to read Hansard tomorrow he will get the answer.

subtopic: MOVEMENT OF UNEMPLOYED PERSONS TO EMPLOYMENT IN OTHER AREAS
speechtext: I think I understood- perfectly well; I repeat the question.

subtopic: MOVEMENT OF UNEMPLOYED PERSONS TO EMPLOYMENT IN OTHER AREAS
speechtext: I should like to direct a question, to the Minister of Labour. Does the minister propose to extend across Canada the policy of providing work for those out of work as is done in Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: MOVEMENT OF UNEMPLOYED PERSONS TO EMPLOYMENT IN OTHER AREAS
speechtext: Because of the noise I did not get my hon. friend's question.

subtopic: MOVEMENT OF UNEMPLOYED PERSONS TO EMPLOYMENT IN OTHER AREAS
speechtext: Does the minister propose to extend the policy across Canada which has been extended to those unemployed in Nova Scotia, or is it limited to Nova Scotia and the mines?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: MOVEMENT OF UNEMPLOYED PERSONS TO EMPLOYMENT IN OTHER AREAS
speechtext:
I do not think anyone can accuse me of not speaking loudly enough.
I think I answered that question previously. There has to be common sense in this thing. Before I came to the government I had experience in moving people at the expense of the government, particularly in the pre-war days. We picked out certain areas where the situation was difficult, such as the Cape Breton area, and Halifax, and Vancouver fifteen months ago, as I said. By the very nature of things I do not think it is financially possible for any government to bear the expense of everybody who wants to move from one place to another, and I am sure my hon. friend will see the difficulties and complications that would arise if it were made a universal policy.

subtopic: MOVEMENT OF UNEMPLOYED PERSONS TO EMPLOYMENT IN OTHER AREAS
speechtext: You still have the ambassador cure for unemployment.

subtopic: CONVICTION OF BRITISH WAR BRIDE UNDER LIQUOR REGULATIONS

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: CONVICTION OF BRITISH WAR BRIDE UNDER LIQUOR REGULATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, last Monday I asked a question of the Minister of Mines and Resources regarding the British war bride of an Indian service man who had been convicted of an offence under the Indian Act. Is the minister now in a position to say what the government proposes to do in regard thereto?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. GLEN (Minister of Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
subtopic: CONVICTION OF BRITISH WAR BRIDE UNDER LIQUOR REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I promised I would give an answer to the hon. gentleman to the question he raised on April 14 regarding the status of a- British war bride who was convicted of an offence under the Indian Act. This is a case in which a white woman married an Indian and consequently acquired Indian status under the provisions of the Indian Act, section 2(d) (iii). This section is the one dealing with the status of an Indian. It is clear from this definition that any woman who marries an Indian thereby assumes the status of her husband. Under section 128 of the Indian Act it is an offence for an Indian to be in pos-

Emergency Powers
session of liquor. This woman was prosecuted for having liquor illegally in her possession and the provincial magistrate wdio tried the case had no option but to convict her. A minimum fine was imposed.
The Citizenship Act does not apply to this case. I have no doubt that when the special joint committee now inquiring into Indian affairs directs its attention to a revision of the act, consideration will be given to recommending amendments to deal with cases of the kind. I may add that the question of the remission of the fine in this particular case will receive consideration.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed from Thursday, April 17, consideration in committee of Bill No. 104, to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council for a limited period during the national emergency, arising out of the -war-Mr. Ilsley- Mr. Golding in the chair.
On P.C. 394.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Carried.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
No, it is not carried. I
presume we are dealing with the Department of Finance, P.C. 394, anthracite coal-importation exempted from customs duty, et cetera. As I understand this order in council, it makes provision for the importation of anthracite coal duty free if it is carried by boat from the United States and deposited in any port in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia or Prince Edward Island. It is hard to understand why this order in council should be carried forward in view of the announcement made by the Minister of Finance in the house a few days ago that all subsidies on imported coal were discontinued. That announcement meant that in Ontario and Quebec the price of coal imported from the United States, which they largely use, has increased from S3 to $4 a ton. Coal imported into Nova Scotia and New Brunswick duty free is taken there in direct competition with the basic industry of Nova Scotia and to some extent with the basic industry of New Brunswick.
With the situation as it is at the present time in all the coal fields of the maritimes, as a maritime representative I strenuously object to retaining this order in council. In view of the struggle which is taking place there at the present time my assumption is that this order in council is retained specifically

for the purpose of helping to defeat the workers who are engaged in a struggle to attain a decent standard of living. That is my assumption, and I object strenuously to it.
Without going into the merits or demerits of the strike I wish to say that yesterday in the house the Minister of Labour announced that the unemployed war veterans in the coal mining area from which I come, to the number of some 2.600, can be moved to central Canada under certain arrangements. I am questioning whether those arrangements are still in existence. I saw a statement in the Ottawa Journal of April 17 by Mr. MacLaren, of the minister's department, who administered the selective service regulations, to the effect that the machinery described yesterday in the house by the minister for removing personnel from one province to another expired on March 31 of this year.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I should like to draw' the attention of the hon. member to the fact that we decided last night to try to stick to these orders in council. If the hon. member will look at the bill he will see what is before the committee.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I am not going to argue
with you, sir, but I claim it definitely comes under this order in council, which provides for the importation of coal into those coal mining areas, and I am dealing with the question of unemployed coal miners or potential coal miners. So long as the government is ready and willing to bring in duty free and indiscriminately United States fuels which hold back the development of our own industry in that section, the question is relevant to this particular order in council.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is, but not the question the hon. member was discussing before I intervened.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am discussing unemployed miners in the coal mining areas where this coal is coming into direct competition-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is the hon. member not a free trader?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes, I am, but unfortunately the government is not. It has pretty well isolated the maritimes so far as trade is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
We never had trade in that part of the country. As I was pointing out a moment ago, my objection to the order is that it will retard that industry. The suggestion that the unemployed of Nova Scotia

Emergency Powers
should be taken to other parts of Canada is not the solution. Last evening when the Minister of Labour and I got into a discussion on the question I merely stated that there were 2,200-I underestimated the number; I always do-unemployed ex-servicemen in that part of the country. Someone over here said, "Well, they won't work" and the Minister of National Revenue said "Nonsense". I told the minister I could find men if he could find the jobs. As I say, that suggestion is not a solution. The solution is the development of our own resources in that province, but that has been the solution for the last twenty-five or thirty years.
Pious people in Nova Scotia will stand up and say that a public works project should be developed, that moving people out is not the answer. I have been listening to that story by men who had responsibility in that province. I have heard it now for twenty-five or thirty years and I have come to the conclusion that it is desirable, instead of having men, women and children on the streets starving without any income, to take them to any part of the world where they may be able to establish citizenship and a standard of living for themselves. It is time for people with responsibility in the maritimes either to develop the resources of that province and put our people to work, or at least to be big enough to try to shift people to places where they will be able to get an income for themselves.
I seriously suggest that the Minister of Labour reexamine the regulations, because on that question of moving people out of the maritime provinces I do not think he has any regulations today. As I pointed out when the chairman suggested that I was out of order, I saw a statement only yesterday by Mr. Mac-Laren, who administered the regulations, in reference to this very question, pointing out that these regulations had expired on March 31st of this year.
Even if- we did decide tomorrow to shift 2,500 people from the maritime provinces into some other part of Canada where there was employment, I do not think we have machinery to do it, and I am objecting that that machinery was not carried forward under these controls, because I think the selective service machinery during the war did a very desirable and a very good job. The people of this country were rooted, they knew where employment was, and they were assisted greatly from one part of the country to another. We have dropped these controls and are back in the hands of the boss, where he
[Mr. Gillis.)
can cow, where he can pick and choose, and unless you are four feet between the eyes you cannot get a job. It militates against the ex-servicemen in the mine districts particularly.
The minister's statement yesterday was a startling one. Of some 1,200 who had volunteered to go from Cape Breton Island to the gold mines in Ontario only 260 odd could pass the necessary examination to take employment underground. What does that mean? Suppose there was plenty of employment underground in Nova Scotia, the men are still not eligible for employment, and that definitely brings them back into the realm of government responsibility, because if they went into the forces fit for war service and came back unfit for industrial service they must certainly have some pension claim.
That is about all I have to say. I would like the Minister of Justice, who is himself a Nova Scotian, to tell the house why this order in council has been carried forward, which merely means the free entry of American Coal borne by water into Nova Scotia or New Brunswick, in the light of the fact that every other subsidy and regulation that was assisting American coal has been discontinued.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Perhaps I should say a word on the subject, since the Department of Reconstruction and Supply has been responsible for the movement of coal over the past several years. The subsidies on coal ended on April 15 and the result has been a very sharp rise in the price of anthracite in all parts of Canada, but particularly in the maritime provinces. Ordinarily no great tonnage of anthracite is used in the maritime provinces. In Nova Scotia last year it was, I believe, about 80,000 tons. That province has depended to some extent on coke for fuel in the ordinary house furnace. The demand for steel and pig iron has increased so greatly that a new blast furnace has been opened in Cape Breton which will take the entire coke output from the steel plant for the rest of this year. Therefore the alternative fuel, coke, will not be in supply from domestic sources to the same extent as last winter. Under the circumstances, and after careful consideration, it is believed that the duty on imported anthracite which was suspended during the war years should not be reimposed at this time. We believe that the present fuel situation is abnormal, and that relief should be extended in the maritime provinces to the extent indicated in this order in council.
My hon. friend has suggested that this is a detriment to the production of coal in that province. I suggest to him that the two are

Emergency Powers
not competitive. Furnaces that ordinarily use anthracite coal or coke are not suitable for bituminous coal. Therefore he is talking about a class of fuel which is not produced in the maritime provinces, except in the form of coke, and which will not be produced as coke for domestic purposes next year, because of the abnormal industrial demand for coke.
Referring to his remarks about the movement of labour from Cape Breton, the Minister of Labour is here, and he will speak for himself, but it is my understanding that it is the policy of that department to move labour from a distress area to areas where there is a shortage of labour. I am quite sure that provision for the movement of men from Cape Breton did not lapse on April 1 and that if men who are unemployed, for reasons other than being on strike, wish to take advantage of the movement, their applications will be considered in future as in the past.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Under what regulations can they be moved? All the orders in council you are carrying forward are here. Will the minister answer this question? The Ottawa Journal of yesterday, discussing this very question, carried a statement from Mr. MacLaren, who administered the regulations, to the effect that these regulations had expired on March 31. Is Mr. MacLaren correct?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I want the minister to
answer the question. It is very pertinent.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: My hon. friend does not need to worry about this.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I would appeal again to hon. members to deal with the items as we reach them. We may reach an item which will cover the questions the hon. member is now asking, but I would ask hon. members to discuss these items as they appear. That is necessary if we wish to make any progress.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: There is no item in this under which I can ask the question.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
For many years I have had a furnace in my home going during the spring, the autumn and the winter, and I cannot agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton South when he says that the anthracite coal which comes to this country is in competition with bituminous coal from the maritimes. The bituminous coal can never take the place of anthracite coal for the heating of houses. Nor can coke ever take the place of anthracite coal. The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply has referred to coke taking the place of anthracite coal, but coke can never do that
in the furnaces in homes and apartment houses in the maritimes, particularly in the smaller places.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I wish to explain a situation in regard to the maritimes. As I see it, P.C. 394 is not a subsidy. It is merely taking off a tariff and continuing it off. That is what we have been asking for for years in the maritimes. For many years in southwest Nova Scotia we have been importing American anthracite coal. If we are to ship out lumber and laths we cannot have the hulls returning empty; we must bring something back. So we used to bring back anthracite. It is just a straight trade. We have built up a certain demand for anthracite. I should not think it will increase, because as a matter of fact oil is coming in. Nevertheless customers of the coal merchants who are buying anthracite today will need anthracite in the future to meet their requirements, because their heating equipment is of such a type that it must have anthracite. Naturally we use a great deal of Nova Scotia coal all over Nova Scotia. But all I can say is that P.C. 394 is helping Nova Scotians and not hindering them. I hope it will continue for all time and that some other tariffs will come off too.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Did I understand the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply to say that ini ordinary heating boilers such as those we use in Toronto, Nova Scotia coal cannot be used?
Mr. HOW'E: I should not like to generalize. It depends on the heating unit. But in a small heating unit in a small house I should presume that Nova Scotia coal would not be suitable. I think the hon. member for Cape Breton South will support me in that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Why not coke it?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Coke would be all right if it is available, yes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The minister is correct perhaps to a certain extent when he says that ordinary bituminous coal does not give the greatest satisfaction in the ordinary house heating boiler. But I use a good deal of Nova Scotia coal in ordinary heating boilers by putting blowers on them. As the house well knows, I have been advocating for many years that we build up a big exchange trade between Nova Scotia and Ontario, that we send them a large quantity of our goods and that they send us back coal. In years past we did buy a good deal of coal from Nova Scotia. I have forgotten what the maximum was, but I believe it was one and a half million or two million or more tons. It is
Emergency Powers

some years ago now. I should not like the impression to go abroad that we cannot use Nova Scotia coal in ordinary heating boilers, because by the use of blowers we can do so, although it is not a hundred per cent satisfactory. However, we must have something to burn, and we are glad to get Nova Scotia coal when we can get it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
This order in council as
extended shows the need for the government doing something further every year regarding coal supplies for Canada, so that it will not be necessary for us to send $58 million a year down to the Pennsylvania coal barons in order to aid and assist them. We should be expending that amount of money for coal and coke produced under the British flag, in Nova Scotia, Alberta and Wales, if necessary. That is what I proposed away back in March, 1923. The government of the day opposed it when I urged a national fuel policy, then adopted it by paying a bonus, subvention or subsidy five years later as I proposed. It was the only way to solve the problem of a national fuel supply to make provision for the extended winters, as they seem to be growing every year by two or three weeks. The people in this country have been nearly frozen this past winter, and they have been clamouring for a new policy. After the C.C.F. and their predecessors from 1923 to 1928 opposed a national policy for coal for five years, the government of the day after 1928 adopted all kinds of methods of protection by bonuses, subventions and subsidies. '
I agree with P.C. 394. I hope that the small man will get some relief in his coal bills. There should be some regulation by the government; they should have this exemption from customs duties for coal, which is only a right and proper one. I hope that it will be extended not only to the small man who uses a few tons of coal but also to the retail coal merchant who has suffered a great deal during the war by not having some proper allowance-50 cents, 75 cents or $1.25 for delivering the coal, sometimes half a ton at a time. It is the poor man that needs protection under this measure.
Mr. GORDON B. ISNOR (Halifax): I think the point raised by the hon. member for Cape Breton South is worthy of attention from another angle. Like other Nova Scotia members, I am deeply concerned about the employment situation. But I think I can say this without fear of getting into trouble, that it is generally recognized that the problem as it appears to the average man in the street is one of production. An industry cannot continue to produce less and less and expect to show signs of improvement; and that is the situation which has existed in Nova Scotia and Cape Breton, and the mari-times in general for a long period of years. I think I can safely say, although I am trusting to my memory now, that the average unit of production per man per day has steadily declined during the past forty years, certainly back to 1901. In all lines of business-I am not talking about coal alone-you must produce in order to create employment; and it is that steady decline in the production of coal which has made employment a very difficult problem so far as our mining industries are concerned. Mr. BLACK (Cumberland); I am sorry this discussion has been unduly curtailed, Mr. Chairman, but as far as I can I want to comply ' with your ruling on this very important subject. The discussion has to do with the question of the emergency, and as such I suggest that the widest possible latitude should be allowed under this section. In order to justify the continuance of this order in council the government relies upon that portion of the preamble which states that there is an emergency which necessitates the continuance of this order in council. The discussion that has taken place has to do with that emergency, as to whether or not there is in fact an emergency and as to what course should be followed as an alternative to the order in council. Such a discussion, particularly at a time when apparently it is of very great moment because it affects the people not only the maritimes but of Canada in general, should not be unnecessarily curtailed.

I have here a form headed "Retail Licence Investigation" which has to be filled out and returned to the wartime prices and trade board. It is the application form that a man has to fill out who wants to go into business, but the form is so complicated that many men who want to go into business do not know whether they are coming or going or whether they will ever get into business. I tried to get a dozen of these forms to pass around among the leaders of the different parties so they would know what I was talking about, but the board sent me only one copy. I guess paper must be short there. Here are some of the questions asked on this form:
Will you kindly forward this report to the local office of the W.P.T.B. under whose jurisdiction the above firm is located . . .
And so forth. The first thing they want to know is whether the applicant has been issued a wartime prices and trade board number. This man's answer to that would be no. Then the questionnaire goes on:
Is retail lumber business to be carried on at above address?
His answer to that would be yes. Next:
Is property where the retail lumber business is to be carried on owned outright or leased?
His answer to that would be, owned.
If leased state number of years property is leased for?
His answer would be no. Next:
State size of property.
Then it goes on with a lot of other questions.
Have storage sheds for dry lumber been erected? If so, state floor space in number of square feet.
Has office space properly equipped been provided for?
Is there a sales staff and telephone service available to the public during all business hours ?
Is the office and sales service outlined under No. 6 located at the above address?
How many employees will be on the company payroll?

speechtext: No. It does not mean that, because under the order in council the wartime prices and trade board has power to make orders with reference to the distribution of any commodity. They may make these orders or improve, cancel or amend these orders, and that will go on. That is not affected by this, but the government could not revoke the section which authorizes the wartime prices and trade board to take that action.

I am not quite sure that I appreciate the position the minister puts us in, judging from the statement he has made today. It appears that he is reserving to the wartime prices and trade board the right to change, extend or modify any regulations in regard to price control covered by these orders in council. As a minister of the crown he states that he does not wish to accept governmental responsibility in administering the policy and he is prepared to look askance at the result if this amendment is carried, restricting the power of the government but not the power of the board. If government policy stands for anything it stands, I suggest, for the government taking a definite position with regard to price control and accepting responsibility in this house. I do not think it is very good government procedure for the minister to say that the house is free, that he will hear the sentiment of the house and will accept no responsibility, that we can move an amendment if we like and he will not oppose it but that we must leave the board under these orders in council with untrammelled power. I do not think that is the procedure we should adopt in this house. The minister should either accept responsibility for the administration of wartime control, to rescind or modify any order in council, or he should say, "We are going to go the whole way and take the responsibility of getting rid of the control."

I had not intended to say anything at this stage but I cannot sit silent any longer in view of the statements that have been made. Members of the Progressive Conservative party have been shouting for weeks about too much power being granted the government. They have made speech after speech deploring the wide powers the government wants, and today they are asking that we hand over power to the government to wash out the board whenever it feels like it. We are trying to keep that power in
Emergency Powers

.parliament where it belongs. I would ask my hon. friends to preserve a sense of proportion.

You are more confused
than ever.

Presumably the discussion
takes place now on P.C. 8528, and with respect to what the minister has said, as to being prepared neither to accept nor to oppose an amendment but to let it go through on a free vote, I do not think it alters what 1 have to say touching this particular order because it does not, at the moment at any rate, detract from or add to the powers of control given the wartime' prices and trade board. That is the point I wish to deal with.
I begin by saying that this is perhaps the most important order in the whole schedule. What I have in mind is that it is the one order upon which depend the powers given the wartime prices and trade board to control prices and make rental control regulations. If this order is amended substantially or is cancelled, then not only do all the price ceilings fall by the board but rent control would go too, because it is the wartime prices and trade board that administers rental control. I think therefore that in suggesting, as I intend to do shortly, an amendment to this particular order, it is important that I should indicate first the attitude which I think we should take to this question of control, and the extent to which the amendment I shall propose will go in interfering with or suspending or perhaps removing the power of control.
Briefly I propose to move an amendment to take one step in the direction of restoring freedom without, as I shall try to point out, cutting away altogether the power of com.rol during the period of emergency. For the purpose of this argument I think we must accept the position that the house by its vote on the second reading has adopted the principle of the bill and suggested that there is an emergency and that therefore a measure of control is necessary.
I do not intend to go back and open up that whole ground again. On the other hand, itr what I have to say, I should like it to be clearly understood that personally I do not accept the doctrine of emergency or the idea that we should continue these controls. My own inclination would be not to go that far. But I shall try to make my argument and my amendment in the light of the fact that the house as a whole has accepted that proposition. In rising to move this amendment and therefore to say a word or two about controls, the position which I take is that controls are and must be a restriction of freedom, that what we should do and what I hope to do

by this amendment, is to restore, not only to parliament but to the individual within the country, some measure of freedom and of the basis of his freedom which, as I see it, is the rule of law; in other words, to cut down upon autocratic rule or to use a word which I do not use very often, bureaucratic rule, and to restore the rule of law, because it seems to me that not only do controls limit economic freedom but they must inevitably limit personal freedom.
Dealing with the question of economic freedom and the effect of controls on the economic life of the individual, I should like here to refer to something which was said in this house in 1945 by a member of the C.C.F. party. Speaking of the effect of controls upon, not big business, but little business- the individual man-the hon. member for Skeena in the course of a lengthy speech had this to say as reported at page 698 of Hansard on October 2, 1945:
The process that we see will end up with the state ultimately becoming the sole capitalist . . . The government recognizes that a crisis is still with us and this crisis will continue with us as the jears go by; therefore we are going to see the absolute continuation of government control within private industry.
The reason I refer to this speech is that it was significant because it was made by a member of the C.C.F., a party which advocates the continuation of controls, and yet the party which says, when we speak of the removal of controls, that we are adopting a position favourable exclusively to big business, a. party which represents itself as advocating the interests of the small man as against big business. And yet this member of the party talking about the effect of controls, went on to say:
It is interesting to me to see what is happening to the social groupings because of those price controls.
I am here omitting a portion of his speech but it can be found in Hansard, and I submit that I am not distorting his speech. He said:
Consequently we are seeing the liquidation of the small trading class . . . Such groups as can be seen to the left, the C.C.F. and the Social Credit party, are an expression of protest from the small middle class, such as the small working class . . . From the point of view of a socialist I would say, more power to the government, because it is hoisting itself with its own petard.
What he meant there, taken from the context, is that the government by these controls is driving the little man out of operation, is oppressing him, favouring the big man, and that all these little men, in his view of the situation, come into the C.C.F., the socialist party. That is a member of the C.C.F. speaking about the effect of controls.

Emergency Powers
You are doing a lot of your own interpreting.

I said that any members who wanted to could read the speech in Hansard. If they can get any other meaning from it they are welcome to do so and perhaps to answer; because the confusion brought into this debate by the C.C.F. perhaps does need a good deal of clearing up. In advocating the elimination of controls or now the lessening of controls, in spite of what was said about us as favouring big business- and that, of course, is not true-we are trying to do what we think will enable the small man, the man trying to get into business for himself now, better to do so. That is on the economic side. I said, when I last spoke on this subject, that I was not one who advocated going back to the economic imperialism of the pre-thirties, and we have a well reasoned policy which would prevent that economic imperialism from coming back.
What is it?
We shall be glad to deal with the question later. I do not wish at the moment to deal with it because, as I said, I wish to confine myself to the picture as we have it at the moment.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

In order to ascertain whether or not he is speaking out of turn, will the hon. member give us the substance of his amendment? That would help a great deal in the discussion. He says he is proposing an amendment. I suppose he should have considerable latitude; but the other day, under similar circumstances, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was asked to give the substance of his amendment in order to enable the other members of the house to follow the discussion more intelligently.
Mr. Chairman, I sometimes doubt whether anything one said would enable certain members to follow the discussion intelligently.
Speak for yourself.

I will give the substance of my amendment. My amendment has to do with the lessening of what I may call the bureaucratic powers at the moment possessed by the wartime prices and trade board under this order in council; and I am coming to that part of my speech immediately. I wanted to give what I felt was the economic 83166-140
background of the thing. I wish to speak of the political background. I shall come to that eventually and then move my amendment. The point in my mind here is that the administration of controls, the enforcement of controls, inevitably involves the cutting down of democratic freedom, the lessening of political democracy, in my submission, as well as economic democracy.
Having dealt with the economic side of it, I wish now to come to the political side, and that is the point I wish to make here. Again we find confusion. We find the C.C.F. and ourselves saying that we believe in democracy; yet one says that democracy can best be served by controls and the other says that democracy can best be served by freedom, by eliminating controls. It seems to me then that we must be in disagreement as to what we mean by democracy, because certainly we both know what we mean by controls. We find that under controls-and this is the point which the C.C.F. party I think agrees with-inevitably the right of the individual to have recourse to the courts, to assert his freedom, is denied; because if, as a part of the plan, the individual must be forced to do this or that economic or personal action, then of course he cannot be free to go to the court and say, "I should not be forced to do this or that, or to take this or that step." If your plan is to work, you must curtail the rights of the individual. It seems to me that controls cannot work otherwise. Indeed it seems to me that at the moment the trouble with the control policy of the government, or the stage at which it has arrived, is that it is only half a plan. It is half control and half decontrol and neither half is working. That is why we say the sooner you get rid of it, the better.
But, to revert again to the question of political democracy and its abrogation by controls, I should like to read what they said in Great Britain on March 3, when they were dealing with the passage of two important bills over there, two important planning measures introduced by the Labour government. The government found it necessary, in order to get those measures through the house, to make a vast change in the procedure of the House of Commons in Great Britain.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I rise to a point of order, Mr. Chairman. My point relates to the ruling you have quoted a good number of times, as to whether or not discussion in committee must be strictly relevant to the item before us. I want to make it perfectly clear that we of this group are not opposed to this kind

Emergency Powers

of argument; we like it, but I want to make it clear also that if it is allowed by one group it will have to be permitted to others, and we shall expect to be able to reply. I have no objection to discussing the whole philosophy of controls, and the whole question of political and economic democracy; I should be glad to go into it for days on end; but if the rule is to be applied at some point and wre are to be required to make our remarks relevant to the wartime prices and trade board, then it seems to me that this would be a good place to start.

If I may speak to the point of order, the section of the order I wish to amend is paragraph 15, to be found at page 28 of the consolidated orders in council. The subsections of this paragraph restrict the right of the individual to appeal to the courts against actions taken by the board and officials thereof. At the moment I am trying to develop a case in support of my amendment, to show that, unless this section is deleted, the rights of the individual are abrogated, and that in order to restore them it is necessary to delete this section. That, I think, involves a good deal of argument as to whether or not this kind of democratic freedom should be preserved. Undoubtedly members of the C.C.F. party would say it is more important that controls be maintained and that this freedom be suspended for the time being. That would be their answer to that argument; therefore they would not support my amendment. My argument at the moment is directed toward showing that it is more important that this type of freedom be preserved than that it be taken away. In illustrating my argument, I am referring to the sort of thing that goes on in Great Britain, to show that if you make controls the thing to follow you do interfere with personal and political freedom, whereas if you put personal and political freedom first you would be willing to accept a limitation upon controls. That is what my argument is directed to.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I would ask your ruling, Mr. Chairman, on whether or not we are to range over the whole field of philosophy or stick to the point before us.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
In my
opinion the point raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is quite correct and proper. I rather hesitated to interrupt the hon. member; but, after all, I think he was discussing the principle of this bill, which was decided on second reading. If the hon. gentleman would state or move his amend-

ment and then deal with it, perhaps he would be more in order; but I think the point of order is well taken.

I suppose it is immaterial whether one moves an amendment first and deals with it afterwards or deals with it first and then moves it, but I should be glad to move the amendment now, or to read it to you. It is as follows:
That order in council No. 8528, as specified at page 3 in the schedule with amendments, be further amended by deleting therefrom sections (1) and (2) of paragraph 15.
I move that amendment because, as I have said, the house has accepted the principle that there should be controls. I do not believe this amendment in any way conflicts with that principle, though I may have my own personal reservations on that point. The amendment goes only to the methods of enforcing the controls. The hon. member for Lake Centre has dealt with that question in far more eloquent and effective terms than I could possibly use, so that I need not repeat his arguments. I should like to read the two subsections in question, however, so that the committee itself can make up its mind as to their effect. Section 15(1) reads:
No member of the board and no administrator or other person employed or appointed by the board or acting on behalf of or under authority of the board shall be or become liable to any person for or in respect of any act or omission of himself or any other person in the exercise or purported exercise of any power, discretion or authority or in the performance or purported performance of any duty conferred or imposed by or under these regulations or any regulations for which these regulations are substituted or otherwise conferred or imposed by the governor in council.
Therefore this subsection preserves a member of the board absolutely inviolate from any action brought against him by any individual who feels himself aggrieved by some action by that member of the board in the purported exercise of his power. Then, as though the restriction of action were not sufficiently complete, subsection 2 puts it the other way around. Subsection 1 says that the member of the board shall not be liable for any wrongful conduct in the exercise of his authority. Subsection 2 goes at it the other way and says that in any event no individual shall have any right to bring an action against any member of the board. It reads:
No proceedings by way of injunction, mandatory order, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari or otherwise shall be instituted against any member of the board, administrator or other person for or in respect of any act or omission of himself or any other person in the exercise or purported exercise of any power, discretion or authority or in the performance or purported

Emergency Powers
performance of any duty conferred or imposed by or under these regulations or any regulations for which these regulations are substituted or otherwise conferred or imposed by the governor in council.
There, under these two clauses, you have the most complete preservation of the officials of the board against action in the courts at the instance of a person who feels himself to be aggrieved by their actions.
Complete immunity.

Complete immunity is perhaps an inadequate description. It is putting the members of this board in a position in which, as far as I know, no one except the king himself has been placed in this country, under the legal fiction that the king can do no wrong. But even the king, under the procedure in the exchequer court, usually grants his subjects permission to sue him. The wartime prices and trade board does not grant the Canadian people that right. This amendment does not take away any actual power to control or make regulations or to impose price ceilings or rental ceilings. All it does is to restore to the Canadian citizen, if he is aggrieved in his .person or in his property by those ceilings or by any administrator's order made thereunder, the right to appeal to the courts to preserve his right.
It may be said that,- if he is given that right, they might perhaps upset the whole effect the board is trying to get at. I do not think that necessarily follow's, because if you give the board the power to impose ceilings, then the courts must interpret the regulation, which is now to have the force of a statute, as the desire of the people of Canada to give the board power to make ceilings; and provided that is all it does, the courts wall not question it. But if, in the imposing of those ceilings, such imposition and the regulations thereunder by some wrongful action damage a person in his property or in his individual person, then it is only proper that he should have the right of recourse against the board, and against the official of the board. Particularly it is proper that the individual Canadian citizen should have the right to bring action against a member of the board who is abusing his power. At the moment, apart from any question of expediency or right or wrong, or whether it is right or wrong to have controls, a member of the board could abuse his power, because the section says "in the exercise or purported exercise of any power" he is immune from action. That permits a tremendous abuse and, in my view, there can be no justification for the continuation of that power two years after the war.
83166-140J
I think we have here an example of bureaucratic power. It may be said, and probably with justification, that the majority of the members of the wartime prices and trade board are hardworking, honest and efficient officials. Personally I have never questioned that; but, since they are bureaucratic powers, I do not see how anyone reading this section can deny that they are powers which are not necessary. They are powers which a minor official of the board, one not subject to the control or at least immediate check by (the minister or by the chairman of the board, can easily abuse. It is not fair to the Canadian people to put them in the position where they have no recourse against, not only the chairman of the board and the board itself, but also local officials to whom power is delegated.
I do not want to cover the whole field, particularly in view of your ruling, Mr. Chairman, and I did not intend to do so at the outset. I think this is a most important question in connection with the whole general matter of control. I should like to read what the Prime Minister had to say with regard to the creation of a bureaucracy and the dangers of exercising a bureaucracy and the limitations which should be imposed on it. Speaking on April 19, 1934, as reported on page 2334 of Hansard, in connection with another control measure, the Prime Minister directed the following remarks against the members of the C.C.F. party:
My hon. friend all the time, even in his speech this afternoon, argues for the extension of state functions. How can you have an extension of state functions, let me ask him, without the creation of a bureaucracy? That is of the very essence of it. How can you possibly extend the functions of the state without creating a bureaucracy, and how can this bureaucracy carry out its functions except by the power of might, which is force, and which is always the power behind government and authority when it attempts to administer public affairs by a large extension of state functions? That is the answer I make to my hon. friend and to the members of his party.
He went on to say:
But the whole essence of the socialist state is founded on that, and my hon. friend knows it.
No one knows it better than he does.
And again:
... he knows that Cole has said that the socialistic state will have to have a bureaucracy and be maintained by force.
The decision of the house has been that we shall continue controls, and it seems to me that the only method by which they can be continued is by a bureaucracy. Call it anything you will, it is an extension of state functions or an extension of state planning and control which the Prime Minister himself
Emergency Powers

has said is an undesirable thing. If we are to have it even for a period of one year would it not be desirable to limit the undesirable aspects of that state functioning, of that bureaucracy, in so far as it is possible to do so without rendering the thing ineffective? I suggest that the amendment proposed this afternoon to give the individual who is wronged bjr abuse of the power of the board the right of recourse to the courts cannot be objected to.

The hon. member has
referred to the provisions of section 15, subsections 1 and 2, which prohibit the right of action against members of the board, administrators, et cetera, but would he state whether he believes that other government officials and civil servants should be liable for acts which they perform in the usual course of their duties?

Not personally. My hon. friend knows perfectly well that if a member of the civil service, in the course of his bona fide administrative duty injures anyone, he is not personally liable. But what we have here is an entirely different situation. You can bring an action in court to restrain that official from proceeding with the abuse of his power or to restrain him from carrying on a proceeding, but under this section the members of the board and their officials are given immunities which ordinary civil servants do not have. The individual is prevented from going to court to ask the court to issue an injunction preventing the carrying out or the continuance of the abuse of these powers. The ordinary civil servant is not protected in the abuse of his powers, but the members of the wartime prices and trade board and the officials to whom powers are delegated are protected even though they abuse their powers.
Where does it say that?
I have read the sections and I am not going to read them again. The particular words are "in the exercise or purported exercise of any power."

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Does the hon. member not think the chairman of the board or the minister involved w.ould correct any flagrant abuse of power?

He might, and then again he might never find out about it. The point is that the immunity is there; it is not necessary and it is an undesirable thing to have. The other night the Secretary of State for External Affairs told us how benevolent, how almost paternalistic this government was, but not all governments may be that good.

The Minister of Labour may not always be there, and I sincerely hope he will not always be there. I have reason to believe that that will be the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I will be here longer
than you will be.

Not unless you join this
party. This party is going over there in the next two or three years, so that if you want to stay there you will have to change your mind. However it is not my desire to be sidetracked. I said at the outset that I would try to present my argument in a short space of time. I have been interrupted to some extent by the points of order that have been raised, but I hope I have made my position clear. I go back once more to what the Minister of Justice said in 1934 when he was dealing with a somewhat similar matter. He said that he did not think that we as members of parliament should entrust to the government powers which were wider than were necessary to carry out a desirable purpose. If he is of the same mind today-and I hope he is-I trust he will see no reason why he should not accept this amendment.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Before the
minister speaks, may I say that it would be wise for any member of the committee who is moving an amendment to have copies for the minister and for the leaders of the other groups.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This section has been
referred to, not only by the hon. member for Kamloops but by the hon. member for Lake Centre, during the debate on this measure. I have made some inquiry about the section, the reason for it, and what the experience has been under it, and I should like to say something to the committee. This section was written into the order in council at an early stage in the war, at a time when it was sought to get as good men as possible in the employ of the wartime prices and trade board, men who would be called upon to discharge disagreeable duties which would cause immense resentment and which would interfere with the ordinary established course of the conduct of business. Naturally they considered a situation such as this where they would be or might be exposed to a large number of vexatious actions, both because their reputations would suffer somewhat and because of the interruption there would be in their duties. So this section, against which a strong theoretical case can be made, and has been made, was written into the order. I have made inquiries whether this section has been abused and I am informed that there is no evidence of any abuse of the

Emergency Powers
section. There has been no complaint from business or from persons who have seen the section in operation. Notwithstanding that fact, it is pretty hard to deny that the section goes too far, and I am going to suggest for the consideration of the committee some alterations in this section. It will undoubtedly be contended by the hon. member for Kamloops and others that the section should be deleted entirely.
The first two sections.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Section 15 (1) and (2). But if the section is deleted entirely the officers of the board will be exposed' to proceedings by way of injunction or other proceedings of the type mentioned in section 15 (2). That is a consequence of the deletion of the section which they fear would be serious, more serious than changes to section 15 (1). Certain actions have been brought by way of injunction, and under the practice in the common law provinces at least-I do not know what the practice is in the province of Quebec-it is not too difficult to obtain an injunction for a few days. An injunction is applied for ex parte and the plaintiff takes in an affidavit and gets a restraining order for a while; four or five days it used to be in Nova Scotia. Notice is given to the other side and the question arises whether the injunction should be continued until the trial. But that period of a few days is extremely serious in some situations with which the board has to deal. It would mean that the thing that must be done from the point of view of law enforcement cannot be done if those few days of breathing space are given. Regardless of the merits of the case, and the board may have had the very best case in the world-

If the minister can show that that is so, I think it would be an unanswerable argument, but I cannot visualize circumstances in which some serious consequences would follow through the board's not being able to take action for four or five days. Can the minister give us an illustration of the sort of serious situation that might arise through that delay?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Let me take this case, and I hope my facts will be accurate; they will be nearly so at any rate. In July, 1946, the price ceiling was suspended on jute bags, among a number of other articles. As soon as the price ceiling was suspended, hoarded supplies of jute bags emerged and were placed on the market under conditions of an acute shortage at an extremely high price, a fifty per cent increase at least over the ceiling price that had been in effect. The persons who use those
bags in their business immediately descended on the board and said that this profiteering, the result of speculation and guessing that the ceiling would be removed one of these days when a condition of scarcity could be taken advantage of, must end. Jute bags, although it does not sound imposing, are an important article of commerce, so that the ceiling was reimposed and the price put back to where it was before.
And the source of supply dried up.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The bags were out at that time. Had it been possible for the dealers to have tied up the board by an action for just a few days those bags would have disappeared in every direction at fifty per cent or more above the ceiling price. That is one instance of what might happen.
An injunction was applied for in one case in British Columbia. It was alleged that the legislation was ultra vires or something of that kind and that, notwithstanding this provision, an injunction lay. That was an injunction to prevent any interference with the disposition of used cars at prices above the ceiling price. That action failed because the validity of the legislation was upheld. I have not traced the consequences. The consequences may not have been so serious in that case, because used cars would be such a commodity that not very much might happen in that interim, but we may have to deal with not just an interim period but up to the time of trial.
The officials feel that the remedy of injunction is an inappropriate remedy because the consequences may be serious. That does not mean that there should not be an action for damages in proper cases. There is no doubt that there should not be complete immunity for the officers of the board, and I agree to that extent with hon. gentlemen who have raised this point.
The question I have to try to answer is how far we can go in this system, which is not our normal system, in applying all the normal rules without destroying the effectiveness of the system. I am going to suggest an amendment to section 15 (1) for the consideration of the committee and invite their views upon it. I am not moving it at the moment. I am just putting it before the committee for their consideration:
That section 15 (1) be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"15(1) No member of the board, administrator or other person employed or appointed by the board or acting on behalf of or under the authority of the board shall be liable for any act or omission in the exercise or performance or purported exercise or performance, in good
Emergency Powers

faith and on reasonable grounds, of any power, discretion, authority or duty conferred or imposed by or under these regulations."
That leaves the word "purported" in there. If we take that out entirely it means that there may be actions where these officials, in the discharge of very difficult obligations, may go over the line a little in the interpretation of the regulations. But if we provide that, so long as they do it in good faith and on reasonable grounds it would be for the court to decide whether they have a good defence. At the moment it seems to me that they are not getting more protection than the law should give them for the period of this act. Under the criminal law I understand, although I have not the section before me, that protection very similar to this is given to certain police officers who may make an arrest which they have not the right to make; but so long as they proceed on the reasonable and probable ground of good faith they are protected against action, even, though they make an arrest without warrant. That is what I propose with regard to that section.
With regard to subsection 2, I do not want to give up the prohibition against injunction unless the overwhelming feeling of the committee is that we should do so, because the officials attach very much importance to it. There are certain changes which should be made in that subsection. I would suggest that it be altered to read in this way:
No proceedings by way of injunction, mandatory order, mandamus, prohibition or certiorari, shall be instituted against any member of the board, administrator or other person employed or .appointed by the board or acting on behalf of or under the authority of the board for or in respect of any act or omission of himself or any other person in the exercise or purported exercise of any power, discretion or authority or in the performance or purported performance of any duty conferred or imposed by or under these' regulations or otherwise heretofore _ conferred or imposed by the governor in council.
Two or three changes have been made in the section. I think more by inadvertence than anything else the section was drafted in unreasonable terms. The words "or otherwise" in the second line of the subsection clearly should come out, and it should be made clear that there is no power vested in the governor in council to confer further duties upon the board; that it is solely the duties which have been heretofore imposed by the board.
Does that mean anything more than there have been the prerogative writs in this particular case?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, it does not.
That is the gist of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is what we should like to see from the point of view of enforcement. Many of these sections would not remain in any permanent legislation. I would not ask that they be put in permanent legislation, but this legislation is not going to last very long. I think that to a large extent we are entitled to rely upon the record of the wartime prices and trade board and its staff. They know very well that nothing would be more shortsighted than for them to rely upon arbitrary sections as a basis for the unwarranted exercise of authority, and they have not done so. If they have done so, it has not been brought to my attention, at any rate. I think they have been most responsible in the way in which they have discharged their duties; but this is a job which peculiarly exposes them to vexatious action by disgruntled persons unless they have some protection. I would suggest that they have the degree of protection which I have proposed here, and that it is not an unreasonable degree of protection.

How times do
change. The other day I dealt with this particular section and the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in lachrymose tones and with much breast beating, indicated that all was well; that there was no ground whatever for the objections which I raised to this particular section.
