speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Mr. J. R. MacNICOL (Davenport) moved the second reading of Bill No. 2, respecting a Jack Miner national wild life week.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as an advocate of the conservation of Canada's natural resources and an opponent of their useless and needless destruction, I look upon this wild life bill as being a step in the direction of conservation because it will promote a programme of conservation in a field which has been largely neglected, that of wild life conservation, and particularly that of wild fowl such as geese, ducks and insectivorous birds. I am convinced that when the bill is in operation, as I believe it soon will be, the same results will accrue in Canada that have accrued in the United States from a similar wild life conservation programme. *
Commencing on March 16 last and continuing up to and including March 22, the United States observed a national wild life week. This was the tenth anniversary week of the national wild life programme in the United States. During that week, over the 83166-141J
radio, through the press and on a thousand and one platforms throughout the United States the people of the United States were informed by various wild life organizations, wild fowl organizations, game and fish organizations and so on, of the tremendous and beneficial results which had accrued to the nation as a result of their wild life programme. The society in the United States which promotes and which inaugurated the programme is the United States wild life federation. I am assured that in this country the Jack Miner foundation will promote and inaugurate a similar programme.
Those who are familiar with the wild life problem will remember that toward the end of the last century and the beginning of this century both the United States and Canada were greatly alarmed over the trend toward extinction of wild life. I remember when I was a young lad I read many times that the Canada goose was on its way out, that in fact it was very rare. However, thanks to the wild life federation of the United States andi the programme they have carried out, which included the sending out of literature prepared by themselves and by various United States government bodies such as the wild life bureau, the insectivorous birds bureau, the wild game and fish bureau, the downward trend toward extinction of wild life in the United States was stopped, and it began to move upward until today their wild life resources are of tremendous value. I shall not weary the house with figures. Today I received from the capital of Pennsylvania a telegram signed by Seth Gordon, executive director of the Pennsylvania game commission. It is addressed to myself and reads:
Conservationists generally throughout the United States are greatly heartened to learn that you are sponsoring a proposal to establish a wild life week in recognition of the wonderful work done by Jack Miner. We "wish you every success in this worthy recognition of one of North America's pioneer conservationists.
During the course of my travels in the United States, I inquired in the different state capitals about wild life conservation measures, and I was heartened to hear everywhere that they accorded to Canada's pioneer conservationist, the late Jack Miner, a preeminent position as the originator of the whole continental wild life conservation programme. The late Jack Miner in the early days of this century made two great announcements outlining the means of stopping the downward trend toward wild life extinction. First, he said that it would be necessary to build or create sanctuaries along the lines of flight of wild fowl from their winter habitat in the south to the breed-
National Wild Life Week

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
ing places in the north. Second, he said that the habitats themselves should be preserved and extended.
In connection with the first, he set up his continental example. On his own farm in the beautiful county of Essex he created in the township of Gosfield, some four miles from lake Erie, the first wild life sanctuary, I am informed, created anywhere in America, and that sanctuary has been expanded until today it covers some four hundred acres of land. People come there from all over the United States to learn how to start sanctuaries, and Jack Miner lived to see the day when a line of sanctuaries stretched: along the flight of the birds from the gulf of Mexico right to the Arctic ocean.
I am happy to say, Your Honour, that one of the best wild life sanctuaries in our own north country, not the far north, but still well to the north, was built by a member of this house, the hon. member who seconds this bill, himself a great conservationist of whose work this country should be proud. I refer to the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette).
Jack Miner travelled extensively, inquiring into the natural habitats of the birds in the south and to the north, and to complete his information he started tagging the wild fowl, which when he commenced that work would not amount to more than perhaps half a dozen to two dozen birds; but I venture to say that on this very night there are no fewer than thirty thousand to fifty thousand wild geese flying out from Jack Miner's sanctuary to the lake, and tomorrow they will return. It is one of the greatest spectacles the eye of man can see, forty or fifty thousand geese in the sky, flying in new formations every second, truly an entrancing spectacle. It is no wonder that the national tourist bureau here in Ottawa has said that that sanctuary attracts more tourists than any other single tourist attraction in Canada. That is a credit to Canada's great naturalist, to the man who was preeminently the greatest conservator of wild life on this continent. The information he gathered through tagging the birds, putting bands on the legs of the geese, smaller bands on the ducks and still smaller band® on the insectivorous birds is most valuable, and on many occasions the United States has sent its wild life directors to gather first-hand information from Jack Miner. That was a most valuable work he did and he did it, as we all know, at his own expense. He devoted his whole lifetime to the cause of wild life conservation. It is a wonderful thing to me to see men devote their lives to building up their country as Jack Miner did as a great conservator of wild

life, and in doing what he did to develop one of Canada's great resources he did a valuable work for Canada.
The United States has had some difficulty in arriving at a date on which a national wild life week shall be observed. They have had several different dates in March and in April. I believe one of the latest ones was the 14th of April, but finally they settled on the first day of spring. I am convinced, however, that when we pass this bill the great republic in due course, because of the suitability of the 10th day of April, will fall into line with us and adopt that date, so that the whole continent will be observing the same week as wild life week. I shall do my best to promote the week in which April 10 falls, the anniversary of the birthday of Jack Miner, as the week to be celebrated by all America as national wild life week.
I have received thousands of letters supporting this bill, and occasionally some people would ask me why I did not name some other prominent man, that there were other naturalists. It is true that there were. Audubon was a great naturalist. He was born in France and lived in Louisiana. I read all about him when I was in New Orleans in Audubon park, which is one of the greatest parks in the world. But his conservation was not along the same lines as Jack Miner's. Audubon was a great painter and a great promoter of preserving birds, dead birds, stuffed by taxidermists and kept in museums. Some have asked me why I did not use the name of Ernest Thompson Seton. He too is a great man, still living, I believe, and famous as a writer of stories for children on animals and birds. But Jack Miner was a conservator and in that field he was first and preeminent and has never been surpassed.
Others have asked me why I did not choose some great surgeon or scientist or theologian! It is true that these men deserve everything that we can do to commemorate their work. Take the great work of Doctor Banting, for example, which has been of untold benefit to humanity. He has been highly honoured by his native province and his country. He was granted a large donation and pension by the province of Ontario, and his country was instrumental in bestowing knighthood upon him. These men are all entitled to the honours that have come to them. They -were nearly all educated in universities, but this preeminent conservator in the county of Essex attended no university. His school was in the back woods of Gosfield township; his rifle was his pen, and his traps were his books. From his youth he was in contact with the

wild life of Essex county. He was a crack shot. He could hit a half-dollar five times out of five at a much greater distance than most people. I appreciate highly the privilege which was extended to me by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) in permitting me to second this bill. Before I proceed with my remarks, I wish to pay a word of tribute to the hon. member for Davenport who well deserves it. He is a well qualified man to speak on this subject. Pie has followed a straight line so far as conservation and preservation are concerned. We have listened to him on many occasions giving lectures and talks on irrigation and conservation of soil and so forth. Therefore it is a pleasant duty for me to spend a few minutes of the time of the house on a matter which is very important and absolutely above party lines.
To some extent I am a little disappointed because it was not possible to make this national wild life bill a Jack Miner bill. Perhaps I am somewhat of a provincialist in that regard; but I am convinced that no man living in Canada has done so much for conservation and preservation of our wild life as has Jack Miner. Being a citizen of
National Wild Lije Week

Ontario, naturally I have thought that the name "Jack Miner Week" would be acceptable, but we must also consider other sections of Canada. I presume that is one of the main reasons why the title of the bill had to be changed. But this is the occasion and the place for northern Ontario more particularly to say to Manly Miner how much we appreciate the work of his father in the newer sections of Canada, and also the work that the son is doing at the present time in old Ontario. We must realize this.	We
have been bountifully blessed with the great gifts of nature; yet we are great wasters;' we are wasters of our soil, of some of our rural establishments, of our forests and also of our wild fowl and wild animal life. We should bring vividly and forcibly to the attention of our Canadian people that the time has surely come when every man and woman in the country should be a conservationist to the fullest extent. I speak feelingly on this matter, because only forty short years ago when we went into our new sections of northern Ontario, in the wonderful clay belt, as settlers, we knew to some extent that we had to destroy the forest. But I do not think it ever came to the minds of the pioneers that it would be necessary to slaughter the fine herds of moose that were there and the wild life which was then in the northern sections of northern Ontario. In that section, as in every other section of Canada, we have been wasteful to a very large extent indeed. Of necessity these days are gone. That should be one of the finest reminders to our Canadian people in establishing a week of this kind, so well propounded in the present bill.
If it were possible I should like every citizen of Canada to go into the southern section of Hudson bay and the James bay region in the fall of the year, the latter part of October or the first part of November, where they would see wild geese and wild ducks not by the hundreds of thousands but by the millions. Hon. members may not believe that but it is absolutely true. At the moment we feel more secure, because we know they will be well protected when they reach the southern sections of the United States by the fine organizations which have been set up there to protect these birds. We know what Ducks Unlimited has accomplished in the northern and western sections of the western provinces, and also what it has accomplished in every section of Canada. At one time we were fearful that the wild duck life would be so depleted that it might disappear as have some of the birds which our

fathers knew as part of the wild life population of this country. For that reason I wish to be brief because we hope and expect that this bill will pass with as little deliberation as possible.
I wish to mention again what has been accomplished by Jack Miner. What he has done will always be to us a great lesson in what can be done, and it is being well propagated at the present time by his son. I trust that national wild life week will be taught in our schools, because at the present time there are very few schools which do not include in their curriculum something on con-servationism and preservation of our wild life and also of our natural resources. Without elaborating any further, may I say that it is with the greatest pleasure that I second this bill in the hope that it will receive unanimous support from every section of the house.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to support this bill, I do so not merely personally, but at the request of the mayor of the city of Windsor, and on behalf of the Essex county tourist association and the Essex county sportsmen's association and, I feel sure, on behalf of all citizens of Essex county and western Ontario.
You have heard, during the course of this debate, that the late Jack Miner was a farmer and operator of a tile yard in the county of Essex at Kingsville near the city of Windsor. In his early years, in his desire to protect the wild fowl migrating to the north and south in the spring and fall, he created a sanctuary where, at his own expense, these fowl were fed grain and provided a landing and resting place in a small secluded pond. In order to note the habits of the migrating birds, and to encourage the preservation of wild life, he employed a novel scheme which was destined, in time to come, to make him a world figure.
There are many points throughout the North and South American continents which have been set aside as game sanctuaries, none of which has attained the prominence of that maintained by the late Jack Miner. It is true that the migrating habits at such other sanctuaries have been able to determine the habits of migrating birds in a cold, impersonal, statistical manner usually by the affixing of a band on a captured bird on which a certain serial number is engraved. Jack Miner, however, had a great respect for his fellow man. He had a great love for mankind. His life expressed a love for children and flowers and nature. This desire to be of help to mankind found expression in his scheme of attaching to the leg of a captured bird a little metal

National Wild Life Week
band on which was impressed a short verse of scripture and the name "Jack Miner, Kingsville, Ontario, Canada."
It was not long after instituting his scheme until reports came to him from many parts of Canada, United States and South America of the capture of birds on which bands had been placed. Thus valuable information was obtained for the governments of Canada and the United States; but, in addition thereto, the good will of Canada was spread from Kingsville not only to different parts of northern Canada, but to the eastern part of the United States and to the northern part of South America, including Central America. Indians in northern Canada, upon shooting a bird with one of these bands, would take it to the missionary near them to find out what it was, and the missionary, upon explaining it, would have an opportunity in his work of expounding Christian doctrine. In Central and South America many natives learned their first English words by taking these bands to their parish priests or missionaries for translation and explanation.
Thus it was that the name "Jack Miner, Kingsville, Ontario, Canada," with the comforting and regenerating message, was spread throughout the American continents. But this was not all, for it attracted many of the leading educationalists, politicians, laymen and businessmen throughout the world. It was not uncommon for Jack Miner to have, as guests at his farm, persons from European countries, especially England, some of whom, to my personal knowledge, made the trip specially to visit him.
In time, partly through his geographical location but mostly because of the haven provided by Jack Miner, the birds came to regard the Miner sanctuary as a haven of refuge in their migration and a place where they might find food and rest. Usually the birds, during the daylight hours, remained close to the shores of lake Erie where it is not an uncommon sight, during the migrating seasons, to see tens of thousands of ducks, geese and white swans. Toward twilight the wild geese and ducks and sometimes the swans fly in from the lake to the Miner sanctuary where they receive food and then depart early in the morning. To say that Jack Miner was a local character is not correct, for he was an international figure with friends all over the world who had duplications of his sanctuary in many foreign countries.
The War Cry, the publication of the Salvation Army, in the April 5, 1947, issue says;
Mr. Miner's life was not lived in just his home town of Kingsville, which he made famous throughout the world; but his name was so
much a household word throughout the dominion that when one thinks of birds, the subject is inescapably linked up with the bird sanctuary.
Let it be granted that other great ornithologists lived before Jack Miner, and live today; but their lives centred each around one locality, and what they left behind were, in a good many cases, dead specimens of birds, very rare bird skins for scientific study in schools, or exhibits in glass eases in museums.
Miner's life-work, however, was very different to this. He left behind him living creatures, the actual living birds which our children and our children's children may see in their customary haunts and natural environment, and but for the famous naturalist's foresight and energy might today be extinct.
To-day, because of the fact that Jack Miner lived, Canada possesses millions of living birds because he gave protection to their kind-a sanctuary from slaughter, a haven of rest on their long flight, and food. This heritage of bird life we owe to him, not only because of the well maintained sanctuary at Kingsville, but also because of the hundreds of bird refuges which his influence helped to create.
Jack Miller was, and is, even today probably the best advertising agent that Canada has ever had, for the advertising which he has obtained has been that which no money could buy. Practically every worth-while publication in the United States and other parts of the world has, at one time or another, carried news items and feature articles repeating the kindness, joy and gospel of conservation in the protection of wild fowl as expressed by Jack Miner.
On another occasion, I have had the privilege of referring to feature stories in the Saturday Evening Post, depicting the story of Jack Miner and telling of the attractions, people and privileges of the Dominion of Canada. I need not tell you, Mr. Speaker, of the tremendous circulation of this publication and of the value in dollars and cents to the Dominion of Canada.
The Christian Science Monitor, the great international daily newspaper, has also featured the story of Jack Miner which has been of advertising value for Canada throughout the world. The Canadian Churchman, the national Church of England news review, together with radio station CKLW at Windsor and other leading stations, many leading daily newspapers, weekly publications, magazines, have publicized the work of Jack Miner and the Dominion of Canada throughout the universe.
As I came into the house tonight I received a telegram advising me that in a recent radio broadcast were carried over C.B.C. by Claire Wallace there were 500,000 listeners in Canada -it was heard in 300,000 homes in this country
National Wild Lije Week

over twenty-nine stations. This says nothing about the millions who hear 'her in the United States which they have no way of estimating.
I think, however, that Jack Miner's greatest contribution to Canada from not only a social but a monetary point of view has been his assistance to and interest in the tourist industry in Canada. Last year I am informed that 20,875,701 tourists entered Canada from all ports. Of this number, 5,191,009 tourists entered by the port of Windsor, Ontario. I could quote at this point from the Windsor Daily Star, since this publication is read by the members of the house more than any other publication and is quoted more often, but I will give what others say. I will, therefore, read from a journal published some distance from Windsor and which perhaps is not as widely knowTn. The reference is made from the November 28, 1946, issue of Watson, Sask., Witness'.
Windsor, Ontario.'-With the fall (November) migration of waterfowl at its peak at the world famous Jack Miner bird sanctuary twenty-five miles from here, the custom officers and immigration officers at this port of entry today said that "more people coming into Canada ask the way to Jack Miner's than any other place."
All United States and Canada has copied his bird sanctuary idea for conservation of bird life which is a national asset to this country. Although the late Jack Miner passed on two years ago it is good to know that his sons are carrying on the work more energetically than ever. Before Jack Miner died he said "What made my bird sanctuary such a success was because I took God in partnership with me." He started to put verses of scripture on his bird bands and in this way he secured the cooperation of the Jesuit priest and Anglican missionaries in Hudson and James bay, who acted as his agents in collecting them from the Indians and Eskimos. The verse of scripture on the band gave him the wholehearted cooperation of every church in North America; the banding of birds gave him the support of every sportsman, and thus the place has become so popular in attracting tourists from all over the world.
It is not an uncommon sight to see at the Miner sanctuary 500 motor cars, most of which have come from the United States; and, from a purely mercenary point of view, they leave many valuable dollars in the Dominion of Canada, and you can be sure that a dollar made in the tourist industry is worth every bit as much as a dollar made by growing wheat in western Canada.
Jack Miner passed on at his home and bird sanctuary, at Kingsville, Ontario, on November 3, 1944; but Jack Miner did not die, for the work that he accomplished has carried on and the human endea vour has been propagated in his three sons wl a have been doing the work instituted by the father, and Jack Miner's "Peace on earth, good will toward men" is

still being spread all over the globe through the feathered friends which he made and protected.
Just recently I attended a gathering in Kingsville -which -was the twenty-fifth wedding anniversary of one of the sons, and there, leading businessmen of the United States, educationalists, professional people, radio commentators, editors, and the rest of us common folk, had an opportunity of again paying tribute to Jack Miner through his son. It is therefore my recommendation, Mr. Speaker, that this bill be given favourable consideration by the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. PAUL MARTIN (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I rise to speak for a few minutes, not only because of my own interest in this matter, but also because of the unavoidable absence of the hon. member for Essex South (Mr. Clark) in whose riding the Jack Miner bird sanctuary is situated. I am sure that the mover of this resolution would agree that the hon. member for Essex South has, throughout the years, displayed great interest in Jack Miner and his work. The hon. member for Essex South unfortunately found himself unable to be here tonight to add his voice in support of those who have already spoken. As the speaker preceding me has stated, Jack Miner was not only a citizen of Canada and a well known and useful citizen of the county of Essex, but by virtue of his great work in the field of conservation of wild life he may be said to have been almost a citizen of the world.
Those of us who live in Essex county look upon the Jack Miner foundation and the sanctuary as one of our most important possessions and one in which we have a great and legitimate pride, not only because of its attraction to tourists, but also because of the lesson it teaches to all of us, particularly to the children, of the importance of wild life. Not only did Jack Miner do much for the conservation of wild life; but his fine character, known particularly to those of us who live in Essex. county, was such as to urge us, if for no other reason, to give our support to this bill in the form in which I understand it is to be placed later by the minister under whose department this matter comes. The government, through the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen), has not failed to show its continued concern and interest in the great work of Jack Miner. Under the present Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen), the grant of $2,500 was increased, and the contribution now made annually by this govern-

National Wild Life Week
ment, and through it, by parliament, to the Jack Miner foundation is in the amount of $5,000.
Speaking for those in our county, I may say that we are grateful to the members of this house for that grant and for their interest in this matter. So, Mr. Speaker, in order to give the minister time to speak on behalf of his department tonight, and in order that the bill may possibly be facilitated in its passage, I wish to join with those who have thus far spoken in commending to this house this commemorative week at a time to coincide with the birthday of Jack Miner, a great lover of nature; a great lover of the birds who make our life happier and more interesting; one who by his character was and is a great example, not only to those who knew him but also to those who will read about him in the years to come; the kind of man who made this world a better place in which to live.

May I just say one word. I do not wish to delay the passage of this bill, because I think we all want to allow the minister make his statement and get into committee tonight.
All I wish to say is that I am heartily in support of this bill and of the idea behind it. In these days when the wild life has been depleted in the country, one's mind goes back over the years and one regrets that there was not such a figure as Jack Miner a century ago. Had there been we might still have had the North American pigeon, and the buffalo might have been in greater numbers across the western plains of Canada. Today we have an opportunity of teaching our boys and girls, as they grow up, the value of wild life, through the example of a man who devoted his life to the conservation of the wild life of Canada. On behalf of those around1 me, I have great pleasure in supporting the second reading of the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to support the principle of the bill introduced by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNieol). His zeal and diligence as a member have been most gratifying to those who have known him for many years in our city. He has been a leader in many spheres of public life in our city and has continuously risen in the esteem of his fellow citizens.
The purpose of the bill which the hon. member proposes is to proclaim the week of April 10 in each and every year as the Jack Miner national wild life week, April 10 being the anniversary of the birthday of the late Jack Miner, the great Canadian naturalist who
devoted a lifetime to the cause of wild life conservation. For that reason it is most commendable. However I wish to point out that I think a week is too much. Perhaps there should be a day set aside.
There are educational features to this particular bill. I wish to call the attention of the house and the country to the fact that there has been wilful destruction of our forests. I think of the old country and what has been done to preserve the countryside in many ways. When I visit the summer resorts, I am almost appalled to see the wilful destruction around the countryside of the forests that we used to have years ago in this dominion. There is an educational feature to this bill, because in all the public and high schools and, I know, in the separate schools, considerable time has been devoted to the conservation of this particular kind of life.
I am sorry that more attention has not been given by the chairman and his committee on Indian and Eskimo affairs, and some action taken long ago, instead of talk. If we devoted more of our time to the Indians and Eskimos who devoted all their lives to the conservation of wild life in the forests, rivers and streams of this country, it would be much better. Here we have wasted two years in deciding whether they are citizens or not. They are the very people who saved the wild life in the forests and streams in the days of Frobisher, Jacques Cartier and John Cabot, and of the discovery of Hudson bay, the discovery of the Mackenzie, the Fraser, and the other great rivers that lead to the oceans. While I support the principle of the bill, I believe the time has come when we should really set aside about a day or two to give consideration to these people who have conserved the wild life of the country, who were the original settlers and who were here 180 years before your great race, Mr. Speaker, came to this country, the great French people. Nothing has been done for them to make them citizens and give them the rights of citizens.
I support the principle of the bill. I believe it will have a great educational effect in this country. I wish to commend the hon. gentleman who introduced it-one of the most indefatigable and beloved members of the House of Commons-for what he has done in this country not only for forest conservation and power development but in advancing many of the features of our public life.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. GLEN (Minister of Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry the time is getting on towards nine o'clock because I should like to have seen this bill go through. As the house will remember, last year we
National Wild Lije Week

had a similar bill, and I was forced to take exception to it on the ground that a precedent would have been established in regard to the setting apart of a national holiday named' for an individual in the country. What I said then I would repeat now. I do not intend in any way to detract from the stature, reputation or prestige of Jack Miner, who was a national figure throughout Canada; but I did think at that time, and I suggested to the hon. gentleman who is sponsoring the bill, that the provinces should be consulted in this matter before we took it upon ourselves to pass such a bill. At that time I promised I would communicate with the provinces to get their reaction, and that I did. I sent a letter to the provincial ministers of mines and resources, and from them I received replies in which they expressed their unanimous opinion that it would be unwise to name a bill after an individual citizen of our country and identify his name with it. They were all in favour of having a national wild life week in Canada, in order that the people of this country might come to know just what our wild life means. I am not going to read all the communications, but will ask the house to accept my word that each provincial minister indicated to me that he did not think the bill should be associated with the name of an individual but that there should be a national wild life week.
I have consulted the sponsor of the bill, who in season and out of season has expressed the point of view that this should be considered the Jack Miner bill. I have suggested to him amendments which would eliminate the name of Jack Miner; and, as he said in his address, he has agreed to this suggestion. So I have no objection to the bill passing, on the understanding that I will move these amendments deleting the name of Jack Miner from the four clauses in which it appears, and setting up a national wild life week.

After I spoke last night, I was sent a clipping from the Toronto Globe and Mail of March 15, which reports that a survey had been made of Toronto homes in the lower income brackets, and forty-three per cent of the families interviewed intimated that there had been a decrease in their consumption of milk since the price of milk increased. I was also informed by a Canadian, who was living in Washington at the time of the disorderly retreat from price control there last summer, that he had been in the habit of lunching at one of the well-known restaurants in Washington where a meal cost $1.25, but that, after the lid had been taken off prices, the very same meal cost $2, and of course a ten per cent tip was expected on $2 instead of on S1.25. All along the line rising prices in the United States make it more difficult for people on fixed incomes to get by.
Before the Easter recess, members of the Progressive Conservative party were active in urging the government to retreat much more rapidly from price control. I notice that they were echoing the sentiments of the president of the Robert Simpson Company. I have a copy of his address to the shareholders of the company.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: We have called P.C. 9029, wartime leasehold regulations, and an hon. member has been trying to get up several times to discuss it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I think this question should be disposed of. Other hon. gentlemen have expressed their views and I want just five minutes to state mine. As I say, I was at a meeting in Saskatoon. It was called by officials of this government, officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs. They called together the businessmen of Saskatoon, the board of trade and other citizens and their effort was to get the Saskatoon businessmen to employ old soldiers forty-five years of age, fifty years of age plus. They wanted to get some sort of jobs for these men to keep them alive. Some people suggested various low-paid jobs, and I contrasted to myself the picture of the boys going out in 1914 and coming back, and the boys going out in 1939 and coming back. These old sweats have to face competition from twenty-one year old boys, and I thought

Emergency Powers
to myself, what a hope! In this competitive world today you cannot get business firms to hire people of that kind when you can get men of twenty-one years of age with the potential ability they possess. It was suggested by one person that these men might be able to get jobs paying as much as $30 a month, but the officials of the department did not know that we have in Saskatchewan, through provincial legislation, a minimum wage amounting to something like $83. I am proud that we have that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
When was
that statute passed?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The order that has been lately under discussion is the general order setting up the wartime prices and trade board and giving it its general powers. Order 9029 is the one which clothes the board with certain specific powers in relation to leaseholds. As the committee is aware, the regulations that have been imposed from time to time, starting in 1940, have affected two main aspects of normal leasehold contracts, namely rents and the matter of possession.
I do not propose to dwell on this subject at any great length. It seems to me that we can, with little discussion or questioning, find in this respect the emergency which must be found in order to justify the dominion occupying a field which falls within the ambit of the provinces by virtue of their jurisdiction over property and civil rights within the province. I do not propose to discuss the first aspect of control. I propose to confine myself in some very brief remarks tonight to the second aspect, namely the possession of properties which are under lease or are tenanted.
The general attitude of the government with reference to decontrol in this field was defined by the Minister of Finance on March 25 when he indicated that the policy of the government was for gradual decontrol. I asked him some questions with reference to the policy of the government in regard to decontrol on a horizontal basis, assuming that conditions might improve. They are not improving now; it may be sometime before they will improve in the housing field at the rate the government is proceeding, but let us hope that in the course of time they will improve. When that time comes I asked, what is the basis on which the government proposes to approach the problem of decontrol? The minister indicated that his remarks must be general. If you examine the answers that he gave on that occasion you will find that his remarks were very general, and there is very little indication of the line which the government proposes to follow with reference to decontrol.
The time may come-and let us hope that improvement will come soon; there is little indication of it as yet-when the conditions which constitute the emergency in the housing field will be confined to the urban centres where conditions have been most acute. It may be that in the course of time it will be possible to confine these regulations within a narrower compass. But the steps which the government has taken to date have been in a particular direction. I refer in particular to the step recently taken by the government which is, I think, the first step taken toward decontrol since the freezing order was passed on July 25, 1945. That recent step was announced by the Minister of Finance in this house on February 24. His announcement will be found at page 702 of Hansard. The order of the wartime prices and trade board which he announced at that time is No. 688, dated February 17 of this year. I do not propose to read the whole order; but in essence it has this effect, that in the case of purchases made by the owners of tenanted properties from October 31, 1944, until July 25, 1945-the date of the freezing order-application might be made by such purchasers to the court of rental appeals for an order for possession of the property. and for dispossession of the tenant where it can be established that, having regard to the relative needs of the landlord and tenant for the accommodation and the relative hardship resulting from any order made by them, an order should be made granting the landlord possession of his own property. Then followed this safeguard with reference to time, to be found in section 6 of the order. It provided that any notice to vacate given to recover such possession shall be given in accordance with the law of the province but that in no event shall any such notice be shorter than three months. That was the first step in the direction of permitting owners of tenanted property to recover possession for their own occupancy.
I suggest that a second step is warranted, and the second step will fit in with the announced policy of the government with reference to gradual decontrol in this field. There is a special reason applicable in the case which I am about to propose. I am speaking of veterans who have purchased houses and who are not assisted by the first step of the government in this direction embodied in order 688, to which I have referred. Let us bear in mind that the freezing order was made between V-E day and V-J day, when the great majority of the men and women in the armed forces who were on overseas service had not returned. They were not here to
Emergency Powers

protect themselves during the war up to the day when the freezing order took effect. They were not in a position to compete with other persons at that time in protecting themselves in the possession of property by purchase of it before the freezing regulations came into effect and at a time when they could, on notice, have taken possession for their personal occupancy or that of their immediate families. The notice prevailing generally prior to the period of the freezing order was a six months' notice, accompanied by an undertaking on the part of the owner to occupy the premises by himself or his immediate family for a period of not less than twelve months; and that undertaking had to be given to the rental authorities under the wartime prices and trade board.
I am suggesting that an exception ought now to be made in favour of veterans who have	purchased houses	in	which	to maketheir	homes, regardless	of	date,	and whorequire them for their personal use and occupancy in the same way as owners were permitted to do prior to the freezing order, or in	a similar way, at	any	rate.	I do notneed to go into detail, I	trust, on this subject.
If there is any case which, without further discussion and without lengthy argument, ought to appeal to the fairness of all hon. members, it is the case of the veteran who, returning from service, finds that he has no housing accommodation adequate for the needs of his family and himself, purchases a property and is unable to obtain occupancy of it for himself and his family.
In case any hon. member should raise the question of administrative difficulties in connection with this matter, I suggest that if it was possible to overcome whatever administrative difficulties were created by the promulgation of order 688, any administrative difficulties inherent in the type of amendment that I am now proposing, can be met with equal, if not greater, facility. I would put it to the sense of fair play of all hon. members as to whether an exception ought not to be made from the present freezing regulation in favour of the man or the woman who has served this country overseas in time of war and who has returned to make a purchase after the date of the freezing order of July 25, 1945. As that order now exists, I suggest that it imposes an invidious and unjustifiable discrimination against the veteran. That is one proposal which I make and to which I propose to refer further in a moment.
There is one other suggestion that I should like to offer, though I do not make it now
[>Mr. Fleming.]
for the first time. As a matter of fact, I hesitate to remind you, Mr. Chairman, that I have already made this suggestion, I think, on no fewer than three previous occasions in this house. It is a suggestion which, if put into effect, would, I am sure, provide a greatly increased amount of housing accommodation on a shared basis, particularly in the urban centres. I refer to the necessity for lifting the freezing regulations in the case of tenancies of shared accommodation where such tenancies are created hereafter.
I made this suggestion first in the 1945 session. At that time I made it directly to the present Minister of Justice, who was then Minister of Finance. It will be found at page 3465 of Hansard for that session, on December 13, 1945. May I just read one or two sentences from what I said on that occasion:
May I offer a suggestion to the minister, in the hope that lie may think it constructive. On October 25, introducing certain legislation in respect of housing, the minister said something about the present freezing of tenancies. We know the freezing is necessary in the present situation, but we also know that the drastic freezing order has had the effect of discouraging many people from renting surplus accommodation. One can find many cases, some even in the city of Ottawa, where, to meet the needs of the situation, people would be prepared to rent some of their own housing space, if they did not feel that if they brought someone in they might not be able to get him out, no matter whether he proved difficult or not.
After some further discussion, the minister said:
I will give consideration to that suggestion.
There is no subsequent record in Hansard of any indication on the part of the administration as to its attitude in reference to this suggestion. That proposal was renewed, I venture to remind the minister, on March 25 of this year, to the present Minister of Finance. He took some note of it, but nothing has as yet been done. I would urge upon the Minister of Justice, who is in charge of this bill, that he will make a substantial contribution to the provision of more shared accommodation and more rooms for rent in urban centres if he will introduce an amendment or accept the amendment I am prepared to offer, which will have the effect of providing that the present freezing order shall not apply to tenancies of shared accommodation hereafter created. I can see the difficulties in the way of applying such an order to tenancies at present existing. What I am proposing, as I did in December, 1945, is that for the present this be confined to tenancies hereafter created.
Anyone who has had experience in the administration of the present order well knows that people are not satisfied with it as far as

Emergency Powers
the quite inadequate rights reserved to the landlord are concerned to evict a tenant of shared accommodation.
The minister may say that the order makes provision for the eviction of a tenant who proves obnoxious, but I repeat that anyone who has had experience in the administration of that order knows that provision is virtually a dead letter. It is not simply that it ia exceedingly difficult to get orders under that section of the present regulations, though that is very difficult, to say the least. You have to prove a very strong case, such a case as is most difficult to prove, in order to get an order. It is not only that fact; it is also the fact that the very much restricted rights in that respect reserved to the landlord at the present time have the effect of creating in the minds of people who have surplus accommodation to rent, and who are willing to rent it, the fear that, if they take people into their homes and those people prove undesirable, they will not be able to evict them. That fact alone undoubtedly is having the effect of dissuading many people, particularly in the larger urban centres, from renting space they do not themselves require. I know that in many areas of my own city considerable housing accommodation is available on a shared basis which the landlords would be willing to rent if they were not faced with this bogey that, if they took in people who proved difficult, they would not be able to evict them. I make the suggestion to the minister with confidence that, if he will introduce such an amendment, not applying it under present conditions to tenancies at present existing but to tenancies hereafter created, he will take a long step toward increasing the housing accommodation available on a shared basis. By that one step alone he will increase available housing accommodation, when under present conditions he cannot increase it in any other way on anything like a comparable scale.
I do not ask the minister to take my word alone for this. I am not a voice crying in the wilderness, nor am I offering a novel idea in this respect. I would remind the committee that this proposal has been supported by labour and veterans' organizations, and I am going to recall to the minister two quotations I gave the house on March 22, 1946. which will be found at page 183 of Hansard for that day. These quotations were taken from a Toronto newspaper containing remarks by leaders of veterans' and labour organizations meeting to discuss the critical housing situation which existed in Toronto at that time and which exists today in even more critical form. The first statement was by Major Edwin
Meredith, a leading official of the Canadian Corps Association, who advanced the suggestion I have advanced to the committee this evening because-
-he said he was seriously alarmed about the housing situation in general and the problem of veterans' families in particular.
At the same meeting a prominent Toronto 'abour leader is quoted as having made remarks along the same line. I refer to Mr. Russell Harvey, a leading official and organizer of the American federation of labour in Toronto and a member of the Ontario labour relations board. This is what he is quoted as having said:
"There would be many thousands of additional rooms made available if some assurance were given," contended Russell Harvey of the Toronto district labour council. "The greatest fear of home owners is that they won't be able to get rid of objectionable tenants if they rent rooms that are now vacant."
It seems to me that is a pretty clear case for amendment in order to increase the available supply of housing accommodation. I am prepared to offer separate amendments, Mr. Chairman, in the hope that it may facilitate discussion of these two questions. If the minister is not prepared to accept amendments but prefers to offer his own after consultation with his officials, I should be very happy to put my amendments aside and welcome his. This afternoon I think the minister indicated a desire to meet halfway constructive suggestions for the improvement of these orders, and I hope he will see, in the suggestions I am putting forward, proposals that he may well endeavour to meet halfway. I might just read the amendments I am suggesting as suitable, without offering them at the moment. I realize that if they are to be offered they will have to go in separately, but I suggest to the minister that these are amendments which might well be worthy of his acceptance. As to the first suggestion, namely in favour of veteran purchasers of houses requiring to obtain possession for their own personal occupancy and that of their families, I suggest this:
That P.C. 9029, as amended to date, be further amended by the addition thereto of the following clause:
"Nothing in this order in council or in any order or regulation made thereunder contained shall apply to prevent the recovery of possession of housing accommodation, in accordance with the law of the province, by the owner thereof, where required for his personal occupation and that of his family, where such owner was a member of the forces, as defined in the War Service Grants Act, 1944; provided that any notice given to recover such possession shall be given in accordance with such law, but in no event shall such notice be shorter than three months."
Emergency Powers

May I make just two comments on that proposal. The first has to do with the definition of "veteran". I have taken that from the War Service Grants Act which defines "veteran" in these terms in section 2(f):
"member" and "member of the forces" mean any person who has been on service in the force* during the war which commenced on the tenth day of. September, one thousand nine hundred and thirty-nine.
"Service" is defined as follows in paragraph (i):
"service" means time served on active service in the forces while enlisted or obligated to serve without territorial limitations, or time served on active service in the Aleutian islands.
I am putting this proposal forward for the benefit of those who were absent from the country in the service of the country' and were not here to protect themselves and their families when other people were in a position to buy homes and obtain occupancy before the freezing order came into effect.
The other proposal I have to put forward is in these terms:
That P.C. 9029, as amended to date be further amended by the addition thereto of the following clause:
"Nothing in this order in council or in any order or regulation made thereunder contained shall apply to prevent the recovery of possession of housing accommodation, in accordance with the law of the province, by the landlord thereof in the case of shared accommodation, as defined in the orders made under this order in council, where the tenancy thereof is created after the date of coming into force of this act."
I think that will give sufficient time for the necessary administrative steps to be taken. In order to put the matter on record, unless the minister desires to move an amendment himself, I will move the first of these as an amendment. I do not wish to be dogmatic about the form and I do not intend to hold to my precise wording. If the minister desires to give further consideration to these proposals in consultation with the officials administering these orders I shall be very happy if he will so indicate. I urge, with all the earnestness at my command, that these are matters that are deserving of amendment under the present structure of rent and tenancy control.

case. I will read the first only of these provisions because the other two are ancillary. This is from board order 511 passed by the board under the provisions of the order we are discussing:
Where he owned the accommodation at the time of his induction into one of His Majesty's services and is now a discharged member entitled to the war service gratuity under the War Grants Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I have an interest in this discussion from the fact that the department of which I am minister is responsible for providing emergency shelter. I point out that if the amendment proposed tonight were adopted the veteran would be able to take possession of the house he has acquired within the last two years as against the occupant, who might very well be a civilian, and it would be my job to provide emergency shelter accommodation for that civilian.
The veteran today has all the priorities that the state can give him. He has priorities in the rental of wartime housing and priorities in purchasing houses built under the integrated plan. Those two plans are providing the
Emergency Powers

greater portion of low cost housing. He has other priorities on new construction, and he has priorities in the case of apartments that are built under certain government priority plans. Therefore the veteran has first call on low-cost government sponsored new construction. The civilian has none of these priorities.
I point out to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that the veteran to whom, he refers has been taken care of. The veteran who bought a house in 1942 or owned a house prior to the war is taken care of by an order recently issued, which entitles the veteran who had purchased a house before July, 1945, to make application to the court of rental appeals for repossession of his house and, if he has a case that will convince the court that he is entitled to the house he gains possession of it. That is causing many eviction notices to be given, and I am well aware of those evictions because it is my duty to anticipate the evictions by providing emergency shelter. I could have given the figures hadi I been prepared to speak on the point tonight, but I shall be glad to give them on another day. Many evictions under that order have been passed recently.
But there is a limit to the amount of emergency shelter that can be provided at this time. Buildings of the type we have been converting to emergency shelter are no longer available. For example in the city of Toronto every building that I know of that could be converted to emergency shelter has been converted and the city has extended its activities to far outside the boundaries of the city. If my memory serves me correctly, there are about 800 evictions pending in the city of Toronto as a result of the board's order to which I have referred. I believe they will be taken care of, but almost every eviction today means an equivalent amount of emergency shelter. Usually the returned soldier is living in shared quarters, and the possession of his house therefore means one less housing unit available to the population as a whole. The family formation rate at the present time is away in excess of anything this country has known before, and it is that family formation rate which is causing the lack of housing quarters at the present time. The wartime prices and trade board1, which administers eviction control, and my own department, which administers emergency shelter, are working together to advance this problem of providing shelter for evicted families as rapidly as we can.
I assure the committee that eviction control must be the most difficult control of all to administer. I assure hon. gentlemen that the problem of emergency shelter is perhaps

the most difficult problem that is associated with housing. We are working together. I am happy to say that at the moment we have a roof over the heads of every family in this dominion. There was a time when we could not make that assertion. There was a time, before eviction control was instituted, when we had the papers flooded with photographs of families evicted on the street with no shelter available. Fortunately, through eviction control we have prevented that from happening. That is one disaster that no government can face with equanimity, the possibility of a family, whether a veteran or a civilian having no shelter available, because, after all, human suffering is human suffering. We cannot advance the decontrol of evictions to the point where we have Canadian families evicted on the street without suitable accommodation to go to. That is the practical difficulty in carrying out the desirable proposal of my hon. friend. I can assure him that the officers of the wartime prices and trade board and all the officers having to do with housing are putting forth their best efforts to hasten the day when the step which he proposes can be taken; but I can assure him that, after the most exhaustive study of the problem and from recent discussion of it with my own officers and with the officers of the wartime prices and trade board, the step which has been taken recently is one, the full consequences of which will be felt only over the next four or five months. I can say that it is the considered opinion of everyone closely connected with this problem that that step must be absorbed before any further step can be taken which will increase the number of evictions of families in this country.

I should like to say a few words very much along the same line. The remarks I intend to make are of a general nature and they will apply to civilians as well as to returned men. It is in connection with the termination of leases. I quite realize that the amendment suggested would cover cases, and perhaps an undertaking by the minister that board orders would be amended along the same line would have the same result. I have in mind civilians who have purchased houses after July 25, 1945. The necessity for these regulations is not nearly so great in the country and in small towns as in congested areas. As a matter of fact, when these regulations were first introduced they affected only the more congested areas in Canada. Eventually they were extended to the whole of the country. I live in a small town of about 7,000 population. I

Emergency Powers
believe that if a certain amount of decontrol were effected along the lines which I am about to suggest it would not create a situation such as that described by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply.
My suggestion would be that the order passed recently-I do not remember the date of it or the number of the order-to which the minister and the two last speakers have referred, whereby people who purchased houses between the fall of 1944 and July 25, 1945, could apply to the court or to the rentals administrator to show cause why they should be given possession, should be extended to purchases made after July 25, 1945. There are a number of people who purchased houses after that date without realizing what the law was and who were unawrare of the change which had taken place. Prior to that date, they could purchase a house and obtain possession after six months' notice. I have in mind the case of a young man with five or six children who has been living in the second story of a large building. He purchased his house shortly after July 25. It is a self-contained house. It just happens that the gentleman who occupies the house has two grown-up children who are in boarding school. He and his wife both have a business. They sit very comfortably in this little house. They refuse to give possession to this good neighbour who has six young children and who is occupying a second-story flat. My suggestion is that the order be extended to self-contained homes of a limited value, let us say under $5,000. It could be limited also to rural sections and to small towns. In such cases it would relieve a number of people affected such as the gentleman I have in mind, and it would not cause any serious disruption. It would not mean many evictions, but it would give a certain amount of relief to these people who bought, houses in good faith, thinking that-in the near future they would be in a position to obtain possession.

speechtext:
I have a case which I wish to bring to the attention of the minister. It is an important case affecting a veteran who had a house prior to the war. On his return from the war he was unable to gain possession. I think this case is of general importance. It went through the courts in Toronto, and I have had considerable discussion with the Minister of Veterans Affairs and the Minister of Finance concerning it. It shows the sort of difficulties that we are running into. Here is a veteran, I shall call him Mr. M, who rented this house, say, from the evidence I have here, prior to the war. On his return from the war in 1945 he received an agreement
from the tenant to the effect that the tenant would be prepared to vacate the premises on such and such a date or after a period of so many months from the signing of the agreement. What happened? The veteran asked the tenant to vacate. The tenant said, "No, I cannot vacate because I have no other place in which to live". He took the matter to the court and the court judged that the owner had no right to evict. I shall read the judgment because I think it is important. I took the matter up with the Minister of Veterans Affairs because this man is a veteran. Incidentally I shall send the complete file to the minister when I have finished with it. The Minister of Veterans Affairs said:
So far as this department is concerned, this is not a matter over which our officials have any jurisdiction. I attach for your information a copy of memorandum recently prepared by the director general of rehabilitation in regard to rental control regulations. As I have no information as to when Mr. M purchased the property in question, I do not know whether this order would apply in his ease. However, I shall forward your letter under acknowledgment to the Minister of Finance.
The Minister of Finance took it up and said this:
Mr. M attached to his letter two photostatic copies of a notice his tenant had given him that he would vacate the accommodation. The latest photostatic copy reveals that on April 18, 1946, Mr. R gave notice that he would vacate on or before the 31st of May, 1946. It appears to me that Mr. M should have exercised his civil rights at that time as rental regulations provide that dispossession is under provincial law if the tenant
"has given to the landlord, after the making of the lease for the accommodation, but not as a term of the lease or a condition of obtaining it, a written notice of his intention to vacate the accommodation on a stated date, and has failed to so vacate."
That is the end of the legal quotation. Then the minister says:
However, there is a possibility that Mr. M may have, after May 31, 1946, again created the relationship of landlord and tenant. If so, in my opinion, he would then come under rental regulations.
They took the matter to the court in Toronto and judgment w7as given against the landlord in the following terms; I think it is rather interesting:
Like most of these cases, both parties are urgently in need of the accommodation, and it will be a hardship if the case is decided against either of them, but of course, I have to decide the case according to the law.
The tenant is a monthly tenant of the landlord and on December 7, 1945, signed a notice addressed to the landlord in these words:	"I
hereby submit notice to vacate and give up the premises of such and such an address, Toronto 9, Ontario on or before the thirtieth of April, 1946, A.D., signed-
Emergency Powers

That is signed by the tenant. If this is a valid notice of intention to vacate, the landlord is entitled to possession. There was, however, a considerable conversation on the occasion when this notice was signed. To begin with, the notice was prepared by the landlord at the dictation, apparently over the telephone, of his lawyer; therefore it should be construed strictly as against the landlord. It does not say he gives notice he is going to vacate, he says he submits notice to vacate, but I am inclined to think that taking the words with the meaning which is closest and most sensible that it should be construed as a notice of intention to vacate. However, it was given under the following circumstances as I find the facts. The landlord said he wanted to get married, and he intended to get married in the month of April, and he wanted possession of the premises. He said he was entitled to a veterans' allowance, through the war, and he could not obtain this allowance unless it was spent on this house, and he needed to have something to show the veterans' authorities that he owned the house and had a right to possession. The discussion was a friendly one, and in a previous discussion the tenant told the landlord that if he -wanted to get married, he would try and vacate the premises for him, and I think on that occasion he meant to, and said he would get out in April, if he were able to do so. In other words, if he were able to find other accommodation. The landlord replied that he would not put him on the street, but asked if he would sign the paper, as he needed it, which the tenant did. That is the evidence, and I do not think it was ever intended or ever understood that that notice should be used as a basis of an eviction application. If the tenant had understood by signing the notice he was waiving his right and protection under the wartime rental regulations, I am quite certain he would never have signed it. Perhaps his unfamiliarity with the law does not help, but I think what does protect him is the fact the notice was given for a particular purpose, and it was not intended by either one of them that it should be used as a waiver of the tenant's rights and as the basis for an application. The situation created by the improper use of this notice was the cause of the tenant giving the second notice, and therefore I find it must not be regarded as a notice of intention to vacate. For these reasons the application will be dismissed.
That, Mr. Chairman, is an involved case but it shows, I believe, the length to which veteran owners are put in the effort to regain possession of their own houses. Here apparently was a man owning a house before he enlisted. He is unknown to me, but I give the facts as I read them on the file. He went overseas and came back and got married and wanted to get possession of his house. Apparently, from the evidence, he gets an agreement from his tenant that the tenant is willing to vacate. His tenant then refuses to vacate because he cannot find other accommodation, and the court rules that under the wartime rental regulations the signed agreement by the tenant is not a valid agreement.
I would not bring this particular case to the attention of the committee if it were not one

of many that have come to my notice. In fact I have received a great many more of these cases than of any other types of complaint about housing and rental regulations, and I suggest that serious consideration be given to the amending of these regulations to allow a veteran who has had overseas service if you like-I would prefer to leave it at service overseas, men who were out of the country-to regain possession of his own premises.
I realize the difficulty of evictions. My riding is one of the most congested in the whole dominion. No one know's better than the minister of reconstruction and myself the difficulty we have had about emergency shelter along the lake shore area in the three municipalities outside the city of Toronto. I know the situation and I know what we are up against. Here is the case of a veteran- this man happens to be a fit veteran, but I have several cases of veterans who have a disability-who cannot get possession of his own house, even though the tenant is willing to vacate if he can find other accommodation.
1 realize that the question is a difficult one. I realize, as the hon. member for Eglinton does, that you cannot be dogmatic about it, but I feel there should be some amendment to or alteration in these regulations whereby it may become easier for a veteran with overseas service, or a veteran suffering disability, to regain possession of his own house. I will not make any specific amendment, but I wish to put the matter up to the minister most sincerely, because in my opinion it is causing a great hardship. In judging these matters we realize that we cannot have perfection. We are bound to base our judgment on the greatest good for the greatest number, and I submit that the minister and the department should give the most serious consideration to seeing that some amendment is made in these regulations to meet the type of cases that I have brought to the attention of the committee.
