speechtext:
I do not take second place to anyone in the house in my consideration for the problem of the veteran who seeks to reestablish himself in a home. But I think there is something inherent in this whole problem which touches the veteran and all others who seek homes at this particular time.
I am one of those who consider that the continuation of the legislation protecting against evictions and controlling rents is not only advisable but is an absolute necessity at this particular time. But I have come to the conclusion that we have now reached a point where general blanket legislation covering the whole country is no longer able to meet individual conditions. Beyond question, there are in this country people who are taking advantage of the protection of tie anti-eviction legislation in order to keep themselves comfortable at the expense of other Canadians and who could not under ordinary conditions do that, and do not need to do it.
I should like to suggest to the minister that now is the time to consider seriously placing in the hands of someone the authority to deal with conditions where they arise. I am aware of the difficulties of leaving the matter to the local administrator of rental controls. Perhaps it should go to the county court judge. Perhaps it should go to an independent commission. I shall not suggest to whom it should go, but I suggest to the minister and to the committee that the time has come to decentralize authority with respect to this matter and to allow some-

Emergency Powers

one or some body to consider the specific conditions in the locality where the situation arises. May I give one concrete instance, and then I am through.
In the city from which I come, I know of a man who owns a six-roomed house and who is now renting and living in a five-roomed bungalow; there are the man, his wife, three children and his wife's mother. He has on several occasions suggested to his tenants, who are a man and his wife with no children, that it would be possible to trade; and he has arranged with his landlord for them to move into the bungalow and permit him to move into the house which he owns where he would have adequate accommodation. The landlord of the bungalow is in agreement. The houses are both in the same district. There is no difficulty beyond this, that the house which he owns has central heating and no one has to carry out ashes; the other house has a modern furnace.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Which house had the furnace?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The furnace is in the bungalow which he is renting; the central heating is in the house that he owns. I suggest to the minister that the individual who takes advantage of the protection which is in the legislation at the present moment is not worthy of the protection which is afforded. That legislation was not intended to take care of people of that sort. The legislation was intended to provide the maximum of accommodation, with comfort, for everybody in this country. I have cited a specific case. Those people are reputable people who are just being, perhaps I should say, intelligently selfish because the law permits it. But I suggest that we should give serious consideration at this time to some measure of decentralization which would permit the decision, as to whether or not an eviction should be permitted, to be made by a local authority that would be able to view the circumstances as they actually exist. I think we are past the state of emergency when we can simply afford to say, "Because you have been in a house for a certain length of time you may stay there, no matter who else is inconvenienced."

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I should like to align myself behind the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Eglinton, because in my municipality there is a great deal of difficulty on the part of returned men who want to fit themselves back into home life. I have had to do with three types of cases in which veterans have been discriminated against. The first are cases where the veterans come back

and want to settle down in civilian life, and go out and buy homes without having obtained any legal advice. There are a good many cases of that kind. In the second case the veteran receives his gratuity or credit and wants to get himself a stake in the community, so he buys himself a home. In the third case the veteran, through no fault of his own, has become the owner of a home, and finds he cannot get possession. He is perhaps living with his parents or in some shared accommodation for the time being; a child comes along, or a second child, and still he cannot get possession of his home. I have taken up cases of this kind with the rental administration in Toronto, and they tell me that, while there are not too many of these cases, there are some. I personally know of four or five returned men who, by reason of the freezing order are not able to fit themselves back into civilian life with their families.
I quite appreciate what the minister of reconstruction says in regard to the problem, but I do not think that problem with respect to civilians is so severe that these veterans cannot be given some relief. The original order in council came into force on October 11, 1941. We have had it now for more than five and a half years, and it seems to me that by this time we should be able to do something for the veteran who finds himself in this position through no fault of his own.
Then the hon. member for Eglinton proposed a second amendment with respect to shared accommodation, that as of the date the amendment might become effective the law of the province should prevail in respect to shared accommodation. In other words, under that amendment a landlord would be able to take people into his home and, after a certain length of time, get rid of them if they did not fit into the surroundings of that home. If that were done I feel that it would not be very long until landlords would be making way for people in their homes, which would help meet the problem to which the minister of reconstruction referred, and I believe a start should be made in that direction.
In dealing with this order in council, we find that it has been amended nine times; but the order in council and the amendments do not contain the meat of this problem. That problem is contained in the orders which have have passed under the order in council, the residential order, No. 294 and the commercial order, No. 315. In addition, there is order No. 511, about which I had forgotten but which was referred to by another hon. member, and the further order referred to by the minister. So I suggest that something should

Princess Elizabeth
be done to have these orders compiled in some form that would let us understand' what we are talking about when dealing with them. I believe the time has come when these orders, which really form the basis of the problem before us, and which as a matter of fact are not before us at all, should be dealt with and screened, so that what is best in the orders might be retained and what has become outdated and outmoded might be discarded. I am suggesting that these orders and regulations made under the original order in council and amendments be not now passed; that they stand and be referred to some committee in order that they may be reviewed for the purpose I have indicated.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South mentioned one or two points I thought were very good. His way of going at it is a little different from mine, but this is the first time the house has ever dealt with these orders, so that I think he should find some means of getting at the best that is in them. In the past these orders have been like the laws of the Medes and Persians; no discretion whatever has been allowed. In cases which I am not going to take time to recite there have been anomalies and hardships; the judges have admitted this to be the fact, but they have been unable to deal with them by reason of the terms of the orders. In some cases people have given their word to vacate at a certain time or to pay a certain rental for a property. Those promises have not been kept, but the courts have not been able to deal with the situation.
I was very glad to see that section 2 of order 707, passed on April 7, 1947, made some provision for levelling up rents as between landlords and tenants. That matter had been dealt with in the commercial rental order for a number of years, but had been left out of the residential order, I presume purposely. I cannot think of any reason why it should have been left out, except that apparently the administration felt they did not have the staff to deal with the matter. In that respect a great number of anomalies occurred, but apparently nothing could be done about them.
I am suggesting that a good deal of the discretion which should and might have been exercised under section 36 of order 294 by the rental administrator, or the deputy rental administrator in each jurisdiction, should be extended so that, where these anomalies occur, there would be some way of rectifying them.
I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg South that legally no emergency exists today under which these orders in council can be continued. However, we are permitting them to go on the statute books, and it seems to 83166-142i
me that, where any discretion should be permitted in order to meet these anomalies, that ought to be done at this time.
Progress reported.
